```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
options(width = 110)
library(ggplot2)
res <- readRDS("2026-11-15-football-v2/results.rds")
val <- res$validation
# Two vintages of the walk-forward. `ladder` is every variant as fitted before
# the review fixes (the runs the model was chosen on). `wf` is the re-run on
# the fixed code: the recommended model, the reference and the models that
# bracket the reversion. A comparison is always between two runs of the same
# vintage, and from the re-run whenever both models were re-run.
ladder <- res$wf
wf <- if (!is.null(res$wf_fixed)) res$wf_fixed else res$wf
rr <- res$rerun
rerun_set <- unique(wf$scores$variant)
both_rerun <- function(variant, ref) variant %in% rerun_set & ref %in% rerun_set
paired_all <- rbind(
  cbind(wf$paired, runs = "fixed code"),
  cbind(ladder$paired[!both_rerun(ladder$paired$variant, ladder$paired$ref), ], runs = "before the fix")
)
scores_all <- rbind(
  cbind(wf$scores, runs = "fixed code"),
  cbind(ladder$scores[!ladder$scores$variant %in% rerun_set, ], runs = "before the fix")
)
ha <- res$ha
dr <- res$dryrun
dm <- dr$male
dw <- dr$female
rp <- res$replay
gs <- res$group_scan
theme_set(metill::theme_metill())
sex_label <- c(female = "Women", male = "Men")
engine_label <- c(`stan-nuts` = "Stan (NUTS)", `inla-full` = "INLA, full integration", `inla-eb` = "INLA, empirical Bayes")
col_engine <- c(`Stan (NUTS)` = "#1b3a57", `INLA, full integration` = "#c8553d", `INLA, empirical Bayes` = "#e3a857")
num <- function(x, d = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
sgn <- function(x, d = 4) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d, flag = "+")
tab <- function(d, ...) knitr::kable(d, row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", rep("r", ncol(d) - 1)), ...)
variant_label <- c(
  base = "Reference (calendar clock)",
  brk = "Free season-break variance",
  brk_rev80 = "Break + reversion 0.8",
  brk_rev90 = "Break + reversion 0.9",
  brk_rev70 = "Break + reversion 0.7",
  rev80_div = "Reversion 0.8 + division-by-season offsets",
  rev80_mov = "Reversion 0.8 + promotion/relegation shock",
  rev80_sq_static = "Reversion 0.8; strength + fixed style",
  rev80_sq_none = "Strength only (no style)",
  rev80_sq_rw = "Reversion 0.8; strength + style walk",
  rev70_sq_static = "Reversion 0.7 instead of 0.8",
  rev60_sq_static = "Reversion 0.6 instead of 0.8",
  rev80_div_mov = "Reversion 0.8 + offsets + promotion/relegation shock",
  rev80_sq_static_div_mov = "Reversion 0.8; strength + fixed style + offsets + shock",
  rev80_sq_static_div = "+ division-by-season offsets",
  rev80_sq_static_lvl = "+ league-level walks (scoring, home advantage)",
  rev80_sq_none_lvl = "Recommended model without the style term",
  sq_static_lvl = "Recommended model without the reversion",
  rev80_sq_static_mov = "+ promotion/relegation shock",
  base_div = "Division-by-season offsets",
  brk_div = "Break + division-by-season offsets",
  brk_mov = "Break + promotion/relegation shock",
  brk_div_mov = "Break + offsets + promotion/relegation shock",
  base_sq_rw = "Strength + style walk",
  base_sq_static = "Strength + fixed style",
  base_sq_none = "Strength only",
  sq_rw = "Break; strength + style walk",
  sq_static = "Break; strength + fixed style",
  sq_none = "Break; strength only"
)
lab <- function(v) ifelse(v %in% names(variant_label), variant_label[v], v)
# Paired difference of one variant from another on the same matches, as text.
pdv <- function(variant, ref, metric = "ls_score", group = "all") {
  d <- paired_all
  k <- d[d$variant == variant & d$ref == ref & d$metric == metric & d$group == group, ]
  if (group == "all") k <- k[k$split == "all", ]
  if (!nrow(k)) {
    return("(not run)")
  }
  paste0(sgn(k$diff[1]), " (se ", num(k$se[1], 4), ")")
}
has <- function(variant) variant %in% scores_all$variant
```

```{r}
#| label: summary-numbers
sv <- wf$scores
ll <- function(v) num(sv$logloss_1x2[sv$variant == v], 4)
pr_all <- wf$priced[wf$priced$variant == wf$ref & wf$priced$group == "all", ]
rd_all <- wf$rounds[wf$rounds$variant == wf$ref & wf$rounds$group == "all", ]
vs <- function(d, a) paste0(sgn(d$diff[d$against == a]), " (se ", num(d$se[d$against == a], 4), ")")
ps <- val$pred_summ[val$pred_summ$engine == "inla-full", ]
```

## Summary {#sec-summary}

::: {.callout-note}
## Status, 16 November 2026

The owner approved all five recommendations listed at the end of this summary. Since then, on branch `claude/objective-poitras-964871` (draft pull request [metill-is/sports#104](https://github.com/metill-is/sports/pull/104), not merged):

- The model is recorded as **v2.0** and the engine is in `R/` behind an optional league key `engine` whose default is `stan`. No league sets it, so every production fit is still Stan (@sec-landed).
- R-INLA installs on a GitHub runner and fits both football cells there through `fit_league()` (@sec-runner).
- `r nrow(rp$cells)` dates from 2026 were replayed through `fit_league()` with the INLA engine and the unchanged extract and publish code. Production's own stored fit, put through the same code, reproduces what production published exactly. Against that baseline every difference in the INLA output is assigned to a named cause: the team strengths, the home advantage, the match forecasts and the season simulation, plus two that come from the pre-season baseline being older than today's code (@sec-replay).

- An independent review of the pull request found nine defects, none on the Stan path. All nine are fixed, each with a test that failed before the fix (@sec-review). Two of them change the model as fitted early in a season, and one changes what the season simulation sees before a season. The walk-forward, the comparison with NUTS and the replay were therefore run again on the fixed code (@sec-rerun). The recommended model against the reference is `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_lvl", "base")` on the scoreline and `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_lvl", "base", "ls_1x2")` on the 1X2 score, where it was +0.0248 (se 0.0042) and +0.0084 (se 0.0015) before the fix; the largest change in any single match probability is `r num(rr$move_all$max_move[rr$move_all$variant == wf$ref], 3)`. The recommendation stands.

What is left is the switch itself, which is the owner's: `engine: inla` for football, INLA under `Suggests` with its repository in four workflows, and the six-week Stan shadow from the first 2027 fixture. v2.0 is provisional and is due a re-examination on 2027 matches by 15 July 2027 (@sec-model).
:::

**The four acceptance criteria for moving football to INLA** (@sec-accept): (a) one identical model agrees in both engines to about 0.01: met on the average difference, with single matches over it by no more than two runs of NUTS differ; (b) the same in the hard regimes: met for the Icelandic cells as they stand, not to the same standard with only one season of history; (c) season-simulation outputs agree with NUTS: met, under full integration and under empirical Bayes; (d) walk-forward log score no worse than production: met on the point estimate, with intervals that include a small loss.

**Recommendation.** Replace the football model with an independent-Poisson model that has two intercepts, one weekly strength walk per team with reversion at the season break, a fixed style value per team, a league-wide scoring level and home advantage that walk over time, and pooled sign-free team home-advantage deviations; fit it with R-INLA and keep a Stan program of the same specification as the reference check. The evidence follows, then the plan. No production behaviour was changed by this work: the engine is in the package, and no league uses it.

- **The engine gate is passed.** One specification was fitted by NUTS and by INLA from the same object (results to 31 July 2026). Entry-level and innovation sds agree within 1 % (for example 0.0435 against 0.0432); state posterior means differ by about 0.06 of a posterior sd; held-out match probabilities differ by `r num(mean(ps$mean_abs_dp), 3)` on average and `r num(max(ps$max_abs_dp), 3)` at most; no score difference exceeds one standard error. The one visible departure is the near-zero sd of the team home-advantage deviations, which INLA puts 5 % to 30 % higher. NUTS on this specification needs 63 leapfrog steps per iteration with no divergences (@sec-validation).
- **Walk-forward, 2022 to 2026.** Weekly leak-free refits, `r format(sum(wf$scores_sex$n[wf$scores_sex$variant == wf$ref]), big.mark = ",")` predicted matches. The validated reference specification scores a 1X2 log loss of `r ll("base")`; the recommended model `r ll(wf$ref)`. Its mean home-win probability is `r num(sv$p_home[sv$variant == wf$ref], 3)` where `r num(sv$obs_home[sv$variant == wf$ref], 3)` occurred (@sec-wf).
- **Against production and the bookmaker, 2026.** On `r pr_all$n[1]` priced matches the recommended model's log loss is `r num(pr_all$logloss_model[1], 3)`, production's `r num(pr_all$logloss_other[pr_all$against == "prod"], 3)` and the de-vigged Lengjan line's `r num(pr_all$logloss_other[pr_all$against == "line"], 3)`: `r vs(pr_all, "prod")` against production, `r vs(pr_all, "line")` against the line. On `r rd_all$n[1]` pre-round forecasts, where horizons are comparable, it is `r vs(rd_all, "prodround")` against production. Production's mean home-win probability on the priced matches was `r num(pr_all$phome_other[pr_all$against == "prod"], 3)`, the new model's `r num(pr_all$phome_model[1], 3)`, the line's `r num(pr_all$phome_other[pr_all$against == "line"], 3)`; `r num(pr_all$obs_home[1], 3)` occurred. Ahead of production by 1.3 to 1.6 standard errors, behind the line by about one: suggestive against production, not established.
- **What the structural tests kept.** Reversion at the season break (scoreline `r pdv("brk_rev80", "base")` with attack and defence walks; `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_lvl", "sq_static_lvl")` inside the recommended model); by far the largest effect, one strength walk plus a fixed style in place of separate attack and defence walks (1X2 `r pdv("rev80_sq_static", "brk_rev80", "ls_1x2")`, scoreline `r pdv("rev80_sq_static", "brk_rev80")`); and league-wide scoring and home-advantage walks (scoreline `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_lvl", "rev80_sq_static")`), without which that model under-predicts goals by 4 %. Rejected: a free season-break variance and a promotion and relegation shock. Division-by-season offsets score the same as the league walks (scoreline `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_div", "rev80_sq_static_lvl")` against them); the walks are preferred on other grounds, given below. The style term earns its place on the scoreline, not on the 1X2 (@sec-tests).
- **Home-advantage inflation.** Production's structure makes the team home effects add up to `r num(ha$total_ha[ha$sex == "female" & ha$variant == "ha_a_unpooled_positive"] / ha$raw_log_ratio[ha$sex == "female" & ha$variant == "ha_a_unpooled_positive"], 2)` times the home advantage in the goals for women and `r num(ha$total_ha[ha$sex == "male" & ha$variant == "ha_a_unpooled_positive"] / ha$raw_log_ratio[ha$sex == "male" & ha$variant == "ha_a_unpooled_positive"], 2)` times for men. Either pooling them or dropping the non-negativity constraint removes the inflation on its own; a common volatility does not affect it. The cause is a floor at zero under unpooled, noisy estimates (@sec-ha).
- **Cutover.** The extract, publish and simulation layers read a fit through one method and a fixed set of variable names. An adapter presents INLA's draws under those names, so those layers need no change: a dry run of the whole chain on two dates produced every extract file and `r dm$schema$n_passed + dw$schema$n_passed` schema-valid JSON files with production's own extract and publish code. The remaining work is a config switch, a diagnostics gate for INLA fits, INLA on the CI runner, and a shadow period (@sec-cutover).

**The five decisions, as the owner made them on 16 November 2026.**

1. **Model.** The recommended model, as provisional version 2.0, to be re-examined mid-season on 2027 matches it has never seen. The reservation: it was chosen on the matches it was scored on.
2. **Shadow order.** INLA publishes from the first 2027 fixture and Stan runs in shadow for six weeks.
3. **INLA in `DESCRIPTION`.** Under `Suggests`, version pinned, with its repository added to the workflows that install suggested packages. Not applied yet: it changes what four scheduled workflows install, so it goes with the switch (@sec-landed).
4. **Published schema.** Unchanged for now. The attack and defence home-advantage numbers become an even split by documented convention; only the total is an estimate.
5. **Stan afterwards.** A weekly reference fit of the same model, with a health warning when the mean absolute difference in match probabilities exceeds 0.01, plus a CI test against a stored NUTS reference that needs no Stan run (@sec-reftest). A league with only one season of history stays on Stan.


## Acceptance criteria {#sec-accept}

This report is the gate for moving football to INLA. The four criteria set for it, and where each stands. All engine comparisons below are on the recommended model unless stated.

```{r}
#| label: accept-setup
vl <- res$validation_lvl
e26 <- res$validation_early26
e22 <- res$validation_early22
sim <- res$simcheck
rng <- function(x, d = 3) {
  if (!length(x)) {
    return("(not run)")
  }
  lo <- num(min(x), d)
  hi <- num(max(x), d)
  if (lo == hi) lo else paste(lo, "to", hi)
}
full_only <- function(d) d[d$engine == "inla-full", ]
eb_only <- function(d) d[d$engine == "inla-eb", ]
state_rms <- function(v) { z <- v$state_summ; rng(z$rms_z[z$engine == "inla-full"], 2) }
hyp_rel <- function(v, pattern) {
  h <- v$hyper[grepl(pattern, v$hyper$parameter), ]
  100 * max(abs(h$inla_mean / h$stan_mean - 1))
}
sim_row <- function(outcome, comparison, col = "max_abs") {
  x <- unlist(lapply(sim, function(z) z$summary[z$summary$outcome == outcome & z$summary$comparison == comparison, col]))
  if (length(x)) num(max(x), 3) else "(not run)"
}
# An engine difference over the pure-noise level: "half against half" is
# 2,000 draws against 2,000, an engine comparison 2,000 against 4,000, so
# identical engines would give sqrt(1.5 / 2) of the half-against-half figure.
noise_ratio <- function(sx, comparison) {
  z <- sim[[sx]]$summary
  z <- z[z$outcome == "all places", ]
  (z$mean_abs[z$comparison == comparison] / z$mean_abs[z$comparison == "NUTS half against NUTS half"]) / sqrt(1.5 / 2)
}
nr <- if (length(sim) == 2) c(
  noise_ratio("female", "INLA full against NUTS"), noise_ratio("male", "INLA full against NUTS"),
  noise_ratio("female", "INLA empirical Bayes against NUTS"), noise_ratio("male", "INLA empirical Bayes against NUTS")
) else rep(NA, 4)
```

**(a) One identical model in both engines agrees on hyperparameters, states and match probabilities, to about 0.01.** Met on the average difference; single matches go over, by no more than Monte Carlo error allows. The test as I coded it is a lenient one: it asks that the *mean* absolute difference in held-out match probabilities stay under 0.01, on a holdout of `r vl$dims$holdout[vl$dims$sex == "female"]` women's and `r vl$dims$holdout[vl$dims$sex == "male"]` men's matches (results to 31 July 2026). Those means are `r rng(full_only(vl$pred_summ)$mean_abs_dp, 4)`. The largest single differences are `r num(max(full_only(vl$pred_summ)$max_abs_dp), 3)` with full integration and `r num(max(eb_only(vl$pred_summ)$max_abs_dp), 3)` with empirical Bayes, which is over the threshold. That is not the engines disagreeing: two NUTS runs of one model differ by up to `r num(max(res$engine_noise$nuts_rerun_max[res$engine_noise$breaks_changed == 0]), 3)` on a single match (@sec-rerun-engine), so 4,000 draws cannot resolve a single match more finely than that. Entry-level, innovation, break, style and league-level sds: INLA's posterior means are within `r num(hyp_rel(vl, "^(tau|sigma_str|kappa|sigma_lvl_goal)"), 0)` % of NUTS's. State posterior means differ by `r state_rms(vl)` of a posterior sd (root mean square). The reference specification gives the same picture (@sec-validation). The exception is any sd that sits near zero, where INLA's mean is up to `r num(hyp_rel(vl, "^(omega|sigma_lvl_ha)"), 0)` % higher; it does not reach the probabilities.

**(b) The same in the hard regimes: early season, promoted teams, the women's cell.** Met for the cells as they stand; not to the same standard when there is only one season of history.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hard
#| tbl-cap: "INLA (full integration) against NUTS in the hard regimes, recommended model. Early 2026: results to 3 May 2026, matches to 31 May. Early 2022: results to 8 May 2022, one earlier season of data, matches to 5 June. 'Promoted or relegated' are fixtures with a team that changed division at the latest break."
hard <- function(v, label) {
  if (is.null(v)) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  ps <- full_only(v$pred_summ)
  sb <- full_only(v$subset_summ)
  sb <- sb[sb$subset == "with a promoted or relegated team", ]
  if (is.null(sb)) sb <- data.frame(sex = ps$sex, n = NA, mean_abs_dp = NA, max_abs_dp = NA)
  st <- v$sampler[v$sampler$engine == "stan-nuts", ]
  ss <- v$state_summ[v$state_summ$engine == "inla-full", ]
  data.frame(
    Regime = label, ` ` = sex_label[ps$sex], Matches = ps$n,
    `Prob. diff., mean` = num(ps$mean_abs_dp, 4), `largest` = num(ps$max_abs_dp, 4),
    `Promoted or relegated: matches` = sb$n[match(ps$sex, sb$sex)],
    `mean diff.` = num(sb$mean_abs_dp[match(ps$sex, sb$sex)], 4),
    `largest diff.` = num(sb$max_abs_dp[match(ps$sex, sb$sex)], 4),
    `State mean RMS diff. (sd)` = num(tapply(ss$rms_z, ss$sex, max)[ps$sex], 3),
    `NUTS divergences` = st$divergences[match(ps$sex, st$sex)],
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}
h <- rbind(hard(vl, "Late July 2026 (main check)"), hard(e26, "Early 2026"), hard(e22, "Early 2022, one season of data"))
if (!is.null(h)) tab(h)
```

```{r}
#| label: hard-inline
sc_diff <- function(v, eng, sex, col) {
  x <- v$pred_summ[v$pred_summ$engine == eng & v$pred_summ$sex == sex, ]
  paste0(sgn(x[[paste0("d_", col)]]), " (se ", num(x[[paste0("se_", col)]], 4), ")")
}
```

- **Early season, with history.** Three weeks into the 2026 season the agreement is what it was in late July: match probabilities within `r rng(full_only(e26$pred_summ)$mean_abs_dp)` on average and `r num(max(full_only(e26$pred_summ)$max_abs_dp), 3)` at most, and score differences from NUTS of the size that running either engine twice produces (@sec-rerun-engine).
- **Promoted and relegated teams.** Fixtures with a team that has just changed division are no worse than the rest: `r rng(full_only(e26$subset_summ)$mean_abs_dp[full_only(e26$subset_summ)$subset == "with a promoted or relegated team"])` on average in early 2026.
- **The women's cell** is in every row above and behaves like the men's wherever there is history.
- **One season of history is the real hard regime.** At the May 2022 cutoff (`r e22$dims$N[e22$dims$sex == "female"]` women's and `r e22$dims$N[e22$dims$sex == "male"]` men's training matches) probabilities still agree within `r rng(full_only(e22$pred_summ)$mean_abs_dp)` on average, but single matches are out by up to `r num(max(full_only(e22$pred_summ)$max_abs_dp), 3)`, and INLA's exact-scoreline log score is detectably worse than NUTS's: `r sc_diff(e22, "inla-full", "female", "scoreline")` for women and `r sc_diff(e22, "inla-full", "male", "scoreline")` for men with full integration, `r sc_diff(e22, "inla-eb", "female", "scoreline")` and `r sc_diff(e22, "inla-eb", "male", "scoreline")` with empirical Bayes. With so little data the hyperparameters are poorly determined, and fixing them at a point (empirical Bayes) or integrating over them on a coarse design both cost accuracy.

What follows from that: for the Icelandic cells today, with five and a half seasons, INLA is safe in either mode. For a competition with a single season of history, use full integration and check against NUTS before trusting it, and do not use empirical Bayes. It also means the 2022 season of the walk-forward (fitted with empirical Bayes on one to two seasons) understates what the model can do there.


**(c) Season-simulation outputs agree with NUTS when INLA uses full hyperparameter integration; how far empirical Bayes departs.** `r if (length(sim) == 2) paste0("Met, for both modes: the differences are ", round(100 * (min(nr) - 1)), " % to ", round(100 * (max(nr) - 1)), " % above what the simulation's own Monte Carlo noise gives.") else "Run for one cell only so far."`

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sim
#| tbl-cap: "Final-position probabilities from production's own season simulation, run on 2,000 draws from each engine at 31 July 2026 (recommended model). Differences are absolute differences in probability, over every team and place in every published division, and for first place and the bottom two places alone. The first row of each block is the Monte Carlo noise: two halves of the NUTS draws against each other."
if (length(sim)) {
  d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sim, `[[`, "summary"))
  tab(data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[d$sex], Outcome = d$outcome, Comparison = d$comparison, Cells = d$cells,
    `Mean abs. diff.` = num(d$mean_abs, 4), `Largest abs. diff.` = num(d$max_abs, 4),
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sim-top
#| tbl-cap: "Top-division probabilities behind the comparison: first place (the title) and the bottom two places, for teams with more than 1 % under either engine."
if (length(sim)) {
  d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sim), function(sx) cbind(sex = sx, sim[[sx]]$top_division)))
  d <- d[d$nuts > 0.01 | d$inla_full > 0.01, ]
  tab(data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[d$sex], Outcome = ifelse(d$kind == "first place", "First place", "Bottom two"), Team = d$team,
    NUTS = num(d$nuts, 3), `INLA, full integration` = num(d$inla_full, 3), `INLA, empirical Bayes` = num(d$inla_eb, 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

Each engine's 2,000 posterior draws went through the adapter into production's own `extract_football_iceland()`, which simulates the rest of the season once per draw. Over every team and final place, INLA differs from NUTS by `r sim_row("all places", "INLA full against NUTS", "mean_abs")` on average with full integration and `r sim_row("all places", "INLA empirical Bayes against NUTS", "mean_abs")` with empirical Bayes; two halves of the NUTS draws differ from each other by `r sim_row("all places", "NUTS half against NUTS half", "mean_abs")`. The largest single difference is `r sim_row("all places", "INLA full against NUTS")` (full), `r sim_row("all places", "INLA empirical Bayes against NUTS")` (empirical Bayes) and `r sim_row("all places", "NUTS half against NUTS half")` (NUTS against itself). For the title and the bottom two places the largest differences are `r sim_row("first place", "INLA full against NUTS")` and `r sim_row("bottom two", "INLA full against NUTS")` with full integration, `r sim_row("first place", "INLA empirical Bayes against NUTS")` and `r sim_row("bottom two", "INLA empirical Bayes against NUTS")` with empirical Bayes.

The yardstick needs care. Each half of the NUTS draws is 2,000 draws, so "half against half" is 2,000 against 2,000, while "INLA against NUTS" is 2,000 INLA draws against all 4,000 NUTS draws. If the two engines agreed exactly, the second figure would be $\sqrt{1.5/2} = 0.87$ of the first. Measured against that, INLA with full integration is at `r num(nr[1], 2)` (women) and `r num(nr[2], 2)` (men) times the pure-noise level, and empirical Bayes at `r num(nr[3], 2)` and `r num(nr[4], 2)`. So the differences are almost all Monte Carlo noise, with room for a real difference of 0.001 to 0.002 in probability and no more. A probability near one half carries a Monte Carlo standard deviation of about 0.011 at 2,000 simulated seasons, which is why single cells differ by 0.02 to 0.03 even between two halves of the same NUTS fit. Empirical Bayes does not depart visibly from full integration at this amount of data.


```{r}
#| label: accept-d
pw <- wf$priced[wf$priced$variant == wf$ref & wf$priced$against == "prod", ]
ci <- function(d) paste0(sgn(d$lo), " to ", sgn(d$hi))
```

**(d) Walk-forward log score no worse than production on the same matches.** Met on the point estimate, not beyond it. On the `r pr_all$n[1]` priced 2026 matches the recommended model is `r vs(pr_all, "prod")` ahead of production's last pre-match forecast (95 % interval `r ci(pw[pw$group == "all", ])`), and on the `r rd_all$n[1]` pre-round forecasts `r vs(rd_all, "prodround")` ahead (`r ci(rd_all)`) (@sec-wf). Both intervals include a small loss. By cell, the men's priced matches carry the result (`r sgn(pw$diff[pw$group == "male"])`, se `r num(pw$se[pw$group == "male"], 4)`); on the `r pw$n[pw$group == "female"]` women's priced matches the model is slightly behind production (`r sgn(pw$diff[pw$group == "female"])`, se `r num(pw$se[pw$group == "female"], 3)`). Two caveats cut in opposite directions:

- **Selection.** The recommended model was chosen by its score on the walk-forward, and these 2026 matches are part of that walk-forward. Its margin over production here is therefore somewhat flattered. The reference specification, which was fixed before any of this was run, is `r sgn(wf$priced$diff[wf$priced$variant == "base" & wf$priced$against == "prod" & wf$priced$group == "all"])` (se `r num(wf$priced$se[wf$priced$variant == "base" & wf$priced$against == "prod" & wf$priced$group == "all"], 4)`) against production on the priced matches and `r sgn(wf$rounds$diff[wf$rounds$variant == "base" & wf$rounds$group == "all"])` (se `r num(wf$rounds$se[wf$rounds$variant == "base" & wf$rounds$group == "all"], 4)`) on the pre-round forecasts.
- **Production was handicapped.** From 21 May to 16 September 2026 a configuration bug had production training on unfiltered data, so part of the margin is that bug and not the model.


## The one specification {#sec-spec}

The pilot's INLA and Stan models were close relatives, not the same model, so their comparison mixed approximation error with modelling differences. Everything below starts from a single specification that both engines read from the same object.

Each team $k$ has an attack state $a_{k,t}$ and a defence state $d_{k,t}$ on a weekly calendar grid (weeks run Monday to Sunday). For a match in week $t$ between home team $h$ and away team $w$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{home goals} &\sim \text{Poisson}\!\left(\exp\!\left(c_{\text{home}} + a_{h,t} + \eta^{a}_{h} - d_{w,t}\right)\right),\\
\text{away goals} &\sim \text{Poisson}\!\left(\exp\!\left(c_{\text{away}} + a_{w,t} - d_{h,t} - \eta^{d}_{h}\right)\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

- **Two intercepts.** $c_{\text{home}}$ and $c_{\text{away}}$ are the log scoring rates of the home and the away side between average teams. Their difference is the league home advantage, and it is identified.
- **Pooled, sign-free team home advantage.** $\eta^{a}_{k} \sim N(0, \omega_a^2)$ and $\eta^{d}_{k} \sim N(0, \omega_d^2)$ are team deviations from the league value, free to be negative and shrunk toward zero.
- **Weekly states, common volatility.** A team enters at $a_{k,\text{entry}} \sim N(0, \tau_a^2)$ (entry levels sum to zero over teams) and then follows a random walk with one innovation sd for all teams: $a_{k,t} - a_{k,t-1} \sim N(0, \sigma_a^2)$ per week. The same holds for defence with $\tau_d, \sigma_d$.
- **Forward propagation.** A fixture to predict is a state like any other, with no likelihood attached. Its posterior is the last informed state carried forward with the random-walk variance, so forecasts widen with the horizon.

Weeks in which a team does not play are integrated out exactly: a step across $m$ weeks has variance $m\sigma^2$. The model therefore needs one state per team and week with a match or a fixture, not one per calendar week, and it is still the weekly model.

Priors are the same in both engines. A penalised-complexity prior on a precision in INLA is an Exponential prior on the standard deviation in Stan: $P(\tau > 1) = P(\sigma > 0.2) = P(\omega > 0.3) = 0.01$, and $c_{\text{home}}, c_{\text{away}} \sim N(\log 1.4, 1)$.

In INLA the prior precision of a state field is assembled by hand as $Q = \tau^{-2} R_{\text{entry}} + \sigma^{-2} R_{\text{walk}}$ (model `generic3`), which avoids INLA's built-in intrinsic random walk and its different meaning of "level". In Stan the same steps are written as non-centred innovations. A unit test checks that the two encodings imply the same covariance matrix.

The specification is league-agnostic: divisions, their ranking and the offset groups arrive as data, and the only Iceland-specific code is a thin adapter. It lives in `research/football-v2/` on branch `claude/objective-poitras-964871` (@sec-where).

## Engine validation {#sec-validation}

```{r}
#| label: val-dims
dims <- val$dims
smp <- val$sampler[val$sampler$engine == "stan-nuts", ]
```

Both engines were fitted to results up to 31 July 2026 and asked to predict every match from 1 August to 31 October 2026: `r format(dims$N[dims$sex == "female"], big.mark = ",")` training matches and `r dims$holdout[dims$sex == "female"]` held-out matches for women (`r format(dims$S[dims$sex == "female"], big.mark = ",")` states per component), `r format(dims$N[dims$sex == "male"], big.mark = ",")` and `r dims$holdout[dims$sex == "male"]` for men (`r format(dims$S[dims$sex == "male"], big.mark = ",")` states). NUTS ran 4 chains of 1,000 warm-up and 1,000 sampling iterations with `adapt_delta` 0.9 (the prototype's default when this fit ran; every later NUTS fit in this report used 0.95) on CmdStan 2.40.0: `r sum(smp$divergences)` divergences, `r round(smp$leapfrog[1])` leapfrog steps per iteration for both sexes, largest state $\hat{R}$ `r num(max(smp$max_rhat))`, smallest state bulk ESS `r format(round(min(smp$min_ess)), big.mark = ",")`. INLA (25.6.7) was run twice: integrating over the hyperparameters (its default, 45 design points for six hyperparameters) and with `int.strategy = "eb"`, which fixes them at their posterior mode.

### Hyperparameters

```{r}
#| label: fig-hyper
#| fig-cap: "Posterior medians and 5 % to 95 % intervals of the six standard deviations. NUTS and INLA lie on top of each other for the entry-level and innovation sds. For the team home-advantage deviations INLA's interval starts higher: it misses the posterior mass that NUTS finds next to zero."
#| fig-height: 4.2
h <- val$hyper
long <- rbind(
  data.frame(sex = h$sex, parameter = h$parameter, engine = "Stan (NUTS)", lo = h$stan_q5, mid = h$stan_q50, hi = h$stan_q95),
  data.frame(sex = h$sex, parameter = h$parameter, engine = "INLA, full integration", lo = h$inla_q5, mid = h$inla_q50, hi = h$inla_q95)
)
par_label <- c(
  tau_att = "Entry level sd, attack", tau_def = "Entry level sd, defence",
  sigma_att = "Weekly innovation sd, attack", sigma_def = "Weekly innovation sd, defence",
  omega_att = "Team home-advantage sd, attack", omega_def = "Team home-advantage sd, defence"
)
long$parameter <- factor(par_label[long$parameter], levels = rev(par_label))
long$group <- ifelse(grepl("Entry", long$parameter), "Entry level", ifelse(grepl("Weekly", long$parameter), "Weekly innovation", "Team home advantage"))
long$group <- factor(long$group, c("Entry level", "Weekly innovation", "Team home advantage"))
ggplot(long, aes(mid, parameter, colour = engine)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), position = position_dodge(width = 0.55), size = 0.35) +
  facet_grid(group ~ sex, scales = "free", labeller = labeller(sex = sex_label)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = col_engine, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Standard deviation (log-rate scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text.y = element_blank())
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hyper
#| tbl-cap: "Hyperparameter posteriors, same model and data. The empirical-Bayes column is the single value INLA conditions on in that mode."
h <- val$hyper
tab(data.frame(
  ` ` = sex_label[h$sex], Parameter = par_label[h$parameter],
  `NUTS mean` = num(h$stan_mean, 4), `NUTS 5 % to 95 %` = paste(num(h$stan_q5, 4), "to", num(h$stan_q95, 4)),
  `INLA mean` = num(h$inla_mean, 4), `INLA 5 % to 95 %` = paste(num(h$inla_q5, 4), "to", num(h$inla_q95, 4)),
  `INLA EB mode` = num(h$eb_mode, 4), check.names = FALSE
))
```

```{r}
#| label: val-fixed
fx <- val$fixed
ha_f <- fx[fx$parameter == "home_adv" & fx$sex == "female", ]
ha_m <- fx[fx$parameter == "home_adv" & fx$sex == "male", ]
om <- val$hyper[grepl("omega", val$hyper$parameter), ]
```

The intercepts agree to the third decimal. The league home advantage $c_{\text{home}} - c_{\text{away}}$ is `r num(ha_f$stan_mean)` (sd `r num(ha_f$stan_sd)`) under NUTS and `r num(ha_f$inla_mean)` (sd `r num(ha_f$inla_sd)`) under INLA for women, `r num(ha_m$stan_mean)` (sd `r num(ha_m$stan_sd)`) and `r num(ha_m$inla_mean)` (sd `r num(ha_m$inla_sd)`) for men.

**Where INLA departs.** The team home-advantage sds $\omega$ sit close to zero, with NUTS 5 % quantiles of `r num(min(om$stan_q5), 3)` to `r num(max(om$stan_q5), 3)`. INLA explores the hyperparameters on the log-precision scale, where "sd near zero" is an unbounded tail, and its posterior means for $\omega$ come out `r round(100 * (min(om$inla_mean / om$stan_mean) - 1))` % to `r round(100 * (max(om$inla_mean / om$stan_mean) - 1))` % above NUTS. This is the only hyperparameter where the engines differ visibly, and it is the one the data say least about.

Match probabilities differ by `r num(mean(val$pred_summ$mean_abs_dp[val$pred_summ$engine == "inla-full"]), 3)` on average and by at most `r num(max(val$pred_summ$max_abs_dp), 3)`, two to three times the Monte Carlo error of the NUTS estimate. The difference has a direction: INLA gives the home win `r num(d_home, 4)` more and the draw `r num(abs(d_draw), 4)` less on average, the footprint of its slightly larger $\omega$. No score difference between engines exceeds one standard error.

**Verdict.** On this model INLA reproduces NUTS within 1 % on the entry-level and innovation sds (and 5 % to 31 % high on the near-zero home-advantage sds), to a few per cent of a posterior sd in the states and to about 0.003 in match probabilities. Empirical Bayes loses about 1 % of posterior sd and nothing measurable in predictions. The approximation is fit for the daily fit and for the walk-forward below.

## Which change removes the home-advantage inflation {#sec-ha}

The pilot showed that production's team home effects add up to well over the home advantage in the raw goal ratio (0.298 against 0.151 for women, about twice; 0.314 against 0.228 for men, about 1.4 times), and that a lean model with pooled, sign-free effects and common volatility does not. That step changed three things at once. The ladder below changes one at a time, starting from production's structure (variant A: each team has its own attack and defence home effect, forced to be at least zero with a wide prior, and its own random-walk volatility). All four are independent-Poisson models on the same data (results to 31 July 2026), fitted with NUTS at production's sampler settings.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ha
#| tbl-cap: "Home-advantage isolation ladder. Total home effect: the home-match-weighted sum of the attack and defence home effects on the log scale, posterior mean (sd). It should match the raw log ratio of home to away goals in the training data. The right-hand columns are the held-out matches after the cutoff."
ha_label <- c(
  ha_a_unpooled_positive = "A. Unpooled, forced ≥ 0, per-team volatility",
  ha_b_unpooled_signfree = "B. A with the sign constraint removed",
  ha_c_pooled_positive = "C. A with pooling (still ≥ 0)",
  ha_d_common_volatility = "D. A with common volatility"
)
if (!is.null(ha)) {
  h <- ha[order(ha$sex, ha$variant), ]
  tab(data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[h$sex], Variant = ha_label[h$variant],
    `Total home effect` = paste0(num(h$total_ha), " (", num(h$total_ha_sd), ")"),
    `Raw log goal ratio` = num(h$raw_log_ratio),
    `Mean P(home), held out` = num(h$holdout_p_home), `Home wins, held out` = num(h$holdout_obs_home),
    `1X2 log loss` = num(h$holdout_logloss, 4),
    `Leapfrogs / iter` = round(h$leapfrog), Divergences = h$divergences,
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: ha-inline
hv <- function(sex, v, col = "total_ha") {
  x <- ha[ha$sex == sex & ha$variant == v, col]
  if (is.null(ha) || !length(x)) "(not run)" else num(x, 3)
}
ref_ha <- function(sex) num(val$fixed$stan_mean[val$fixed$parameter == "home_adv" & val$fixed$sex == sex], 3)
```

**Either pooling or sign freedom is enough; common volatility has nothing to do with it.** For women, production's structure gives a total home effect of `r hv("female", "ha_a_unpooled_positive")` where the raw goal ratio says `r hv("female", "ha_a_unpooled_positive", "raw_log_ratio")`. Removing the sign constraint alone brings it to `r hv("female", "ha_b_unpooled_signfree")`; pooling alone, with the effects still forced non-negative, to `r hv("female", "ha_c_pooled_positive")`; a common volatility alone leaves it at `r hv("female", "ha_d_common_volatility")`. For men the same four rungs give `r hv("male", "ha_a_unpooled_positive")`, `r hv("male", "ha_b_unpooled_signfree")`, `r hv("male", "ha_c_pooled_positive")` and `r hv("male", "ha_d_common_volatility")` against a raw ratio of `r hv("male", "ha_a_unpooled_positive", "raw_log_ratio")`. The reference specification, which has both pooling and sign freedom, gives `r ref_ha("female")` and `r ref_ha("male")`.

The mechanism is the combination. Each team's home effect is estimated with a posterior sd of about 0.1 around a value of about 0.08, so the estimate is mostly noise. A floor at zero cuts off the negative half of that noise, and with no pooling nothing pulls the estimates back, so every team errs upward and the error does not average out. Take away the floor, or add the pull, and the bias goes. The held-out home-win probabilities follow: with the inflated effects the model says `r hv("female", "ha_a_unpooled_positive", "holdout_p_home")` for women where `r hv("female", "ha_a_unpooled_positive", "holdout_obs_home")` occurred, and `r hv("female", "ha_b_unpooled_signfree", "holdout_p_home")` once either fix is in. The men's held-out window is the exception that shows why one window is not enough: home sides won `r hv("male", "ha_a_unpooled_positive", "holdout_obs_home")` of those 195 matches, well above the long-run rate, so there the inflated model (`r hv("male", "ha_a_unpooled_positive", "holdout_p_home")`) happens to sit closer than the corrected ones (`r hv("male", "ha_b_unpooled_signfree", "holdout_p_home")`). Over the 3,007 men's matches of the walk-forward the reference specification predicts `r num(wf$scores_sex$p_home[wf$scores_sex$variant == "base" & wf$scores_sex$sex == "male"], 3)` and `r num(wf$scores_sex$obs_home[wf$scores_sex$variant == "base" & wf$scores_sex$sex == "male"], 3)` occurred.

```{r}
#| label: ha-div
hd <- function(v) if (is.null(ha)) NA else ha$divergences[ha$sex == "male" & ha$variant == v]
```

**Divergences.** The women's four fits had none. The men's did: `r hd("ha_a_unpooled_positive")` divergent transitions out of 4,000 in rung A (production's structure), `r hd("ha_b_unpooled_signfree")` in rung B and `r hd("ha_c_pooled_positive")` in rung C, the two rungs that carry the conclusion for men, and `r hd("ha_d_common_volatility")` in rung D. A fit with divergences can be biased, so the men's B and C totals (0.218 and 0.220 against 0.228 in the goals) rest on slightly less solid ground than the women's. The women's ladder, with no divergences, gives the same answer, and so does the reference specification, which has both fixes and sampled without divergences for both sexes.



## Walk-forward, 2022 to 2026 {#sec-wf}

```{r}
#| label: wf-setup
sc <- wf$scores_sex
base_sc <- sc[sc$variant == wf$ref, ]
cov <- wf$coverage
n_all <- sum(base_sc$n)
```

**Design.** For every calendar week from 2022 to 2026 that has a match, the model is fitted on results up to the Sunday before and predicts that week's matches, so every forecast is one to seven days ahead and uses nothing later than its cutoff. The training set at each cutoff is production's own (`model_training_results()`, including the training filter). States are refitted at every cutoff; hyperparameters are re-estimated at every fourth cutoff and held at their last estimate in between, so they also only see the past. A fixture is skipped when one of its teams has no match in the training set, which is the rule production applies.

That gives `r format(n_all, big.mark = ",")` predicted matches: `r format(base_sc$n[base_sc$sex == "male"], big.mark = ",")` men's and `r format(base_sc$n[base_sc$sex == "female"], big.mark = ",")` women's. `r sum(cov$skipped[cov$sex == "male"])` men's fixtures and `r sum(cov$skipped[cov$sex == "female"])` women's were skipped; the men's are almost all fourth-division (LD4) matches, a division outside the training filter. The data start in 2021, so the 2022 forecasts rest on one earlier season.

Scores: the **1X2 log loss** (lower is better) is the primary measure; the **exact-scoreline log loss** is the measure for model development, because it uses the whole predictive distribution.

### Scores by model

```{r}
#| label: tbl-wf-models
#| tbl-cap: "Every model run through the walk-forward, same 4,511 matches. The reference is the specification validated against NUTS above; the others are the changes tested in the next section. The last column says whether the run is from the code as fixed after the review (@sec-rerun) or from before; models without a reversion are the same model either way."
sv <- scores_all
ord <- c("base", "brk", "brk_rev80", "brk_rev70", "brk_rev90", "rev80_div", "rev80_mov", "rev80_div_mov", "rev80_sq_rw", "rev80_sq_static", "rev70_sq_static", "rev60_sq_static", "rev80_sq_none", "rev80_sq_static_div_mov")
sv <- sv[order(match(sv$variant, ord)), ]
tab(data.frame(
  Model = lab(sv$variant), `1X2 log loss` = num(sv$logloss_1x2, 4), `Scoreline log loss` = num(sv$scoreline, 4),
  RPS = num(sv$rps, 4), `Mean P(home)` = num(sv$p_home, 3), `Home wins` = num(sv$obs_home, 3),
  Runs = sv$runs,
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-wf-season
#| tbl-cap: "The recommended model by season. The last two columns compare the mean predicted probability of a home win with the share that occurred."
bs <- wf$by_season
tab(data.frame(
  ` ` = sex_label[bs$sex], Season = bs$season, Matches = bs$n,
  `1X2 log loss` = num(bs$logloss_1x2, 4), `Scoreline log loss` = num(bs$scoreline, 3),
  RPS = num(bs$rps, 4), `Mean P(home)` = num(bs$p_home, 3), `Home wins` = num(bs$obs_home, 3),
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-wf-phase
#| tbl-cap: "The recommended model by season phase: the first five rounds of each division, the middle, and the last third (split rounds and play-offs count as late; cup ties take the phase of the league matches around them)."
bp <- wf$by_phase
phase_label <- c(early = "First five rounds", middle = "Middle", late = "Last third")
tab(data.frame(
  ` ` = sex_label[bp$sex], Phase = phase_label[as.character(bp$phase)], Matches = bp$n,
  `1X2 log loss` = num(bp$logloss_1x2, 4), `Scoreline log loss` = num(bp$scoreline, 3),
  `Mean P(home)` = num(bp$p_home, 3), `Home wins` = num(bp$obs_home, 3),
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

### Against production and the Lengjan line, 2026

Stored production forecasts and odds exist for 2026 only. There are two sets:

- **Priced matches**: the decide layer's candidates table holds, for every match Lengjan priced, production's last pre-match probabilities and the odds. Production refitted daily, so its horizon here is shorter than the walk-forward's.
- **Pre-round forecasts**: the publisher's round history holds production's forecast for every league match in the published divisions, made before the round (one to sixteen days ahead, median three to four). This is the like-for-like comparison of horizon.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bench
#| tbl-cap: "2026, the recommended model against the outside forecasts on the same matches. Differences are in log score (positive: the new model is better), with paired standard errors treating matches as independent; the week-clustered standard error is in square brackets."
pr <- wf$priced[wf$priced$variant == wf$ref & wf$priced$against %in% c("line", "prod"), ]
rd <- wf$rounds[wf$rounds$variant == wf$ref, ]
b <- rbind(pr, rd)
against <- c(line = "Lengjan line (de-vigged)", prod = "Production, last pre-match", prodround = "Production, pre-round")
grp <- c(all = "Both", male = "Men", female = "Women")
tab(data.frame(
  Set = ifelse(b$against == "prodround", "Published divisions", "Priced matches"),
  ` ` = grp[b$group], Against = against[b$against], Matches = b$n,
  `New model` = num(b$logloss_model, 4), Other = num(b$logloss_other, 4),
  Difference = paste0(sgn(b$diff), " (se ", num(b$se, 4), ") [", num(b$se_week, 4), "]"),
  `P(home): new / other / occurred` = paste(num(b$phome_model, 3), num(b$phome_other, 3), num(b$obs_home, 3), sep = " / "),
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

```{r}
#| label: bench-inline
pa <- wf$priced[wf$priced$variant == wf$ref & wf$priced$group == "all", ]
ra <- wf$rounds[wf$rounds$variant == wf$ref & wf$rounds$group == "all", ]
pl <- wf$prod_vs_line
```

Three readings.

- **Against production** the new model is ahead on both sets, by `r sgn(pa$diff[pa$against == "prod"])` and `r sgn(ra$diff)`, each about 1.3 to 1.6 standard errors. The men's cells carry it; the women's are too small to say anything (119 and 203 matches). This is suggestive, not established, and production's 2026 forecasts include four months of a training-filter bug.
- **Against the line** it is behind by `r num(abs(pa$diff[pa$against == "line"]), 4)` (se `r num(pa$se[pa$against == "line"], 4)`), where production was behind by `r num(abs(pl$mean), 4)` (se `r num(pl$se, 4)`) on the same matches. A results-only model trailing the bookmaker by about 0.01 is what the literature reports everywhere.
- **Home wins.** On the priced matches production said `r num(pa$phome_other[pa$against == "prod"], 3)` on average, the line `r num(pa$phome_other[pa$against == "line"], 3)`, the new model `r num(pa$phome_model[1], 3)`; `r num(pa$obs_home[1], 3)` occurred. The inflation is gone.

## Model tests on the harness {#sec-tests}

Each candidate change was run through the same walk-forward and compared on the same matches with the model it would replace. Because the candidates are small changes to one model, these paired differences are measured far more precisely than any comparison with an outside forecast: standard errors are around a thousandth of a log-score unit. Each test builds on what the previous one kept. The brief's order was season break, division structure, then strength and style. The division-structure test is reported last here because its first run was void: a sign error in my promotion covariate, found from the implausible size of the result, then fixed and covered by a test. By the time it was repeated the strength-and-style test had been run, so it was repeated on that model.

These tests were run before the review of the pull request (@sec-review) corrected which teams revert, and toward whose mean. Four models were run again on the fixed code (@sec-rerun): the reference, attack and defence walks with reversion, the recommended model, and the recommended model without the reversion. A comparison between two of those is from the re-run. Every other comparison is between two runs from before the fix, never one of each; the figure and the table say which.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tests
#| fig-cap: "Paired log-score differences on all 4,511 walk-forward matches, with 95 % intervals (matches treated as independent). Each row is compared with the model named in its panel. Right of zero is better. Filled points are from the re-run on the fixed code, open points from the runs before the fix (@sec-rerun); both models of a pair are always from the same runs."
#| fig-height: 5.4
pd <- paired_all
steps <- rbind(
  data.frame(variant = c("brk", "brk_rev80"), ref = "base", step = "Season break, against the reference"),
  data.frame(variant = "rev80_sq_static", ref = "brk_rev80", step = "Strength and style, against reversion 0.8"),
  data.frame(
    variant = c("rev80_sq_static_mov", "rev80_sq_static_div", "rev80_sq_static_lvl", "rev70_sq_static", "rev60_sq_static", "rev80_sq_none"),
    ref = "rev80_sq_static", step = "Division structure, league level and sensitivity, against strength + fixed style"
  ),
  data.frame(variant = c("rev80_sq_none_lvl", "sq_static_lvl"), ref = "rev80_sq_static_lvl", step = "Against the recommended model")
)
d <- merge(pd[pd$split == "all", ], steps, by = c("variant", "ref"))
d$metric <- factor(ifelse(d$metric == "ls_1x2", "1X2 log score", "Exact-scoreline log score"), c("1X2 log score", "Exact-scoreline log score"))
d$label <- factor(lab(d$variant), rev(unique(lab(steps$variant))))
d$step <- factor(d$step, unique(steps$step))
ggplot(d, aes(diff, label)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi, shape = runs), colour = "#1b3a57", fill = "white", size = 0.35) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`fixed code` = 16, `before the fix` = 21), name = NULL) +
  facet_grid(step ~ metric, scales = "free", space = "free_y", labeller = label_wrap_gen(24)) +
  labs(x = "Paired difference (log-score units)", y = NULL) +
  theme(strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0), legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Paired differences by sex and by season phase. Standard error in brackets. Positive: better than the model in the 'Against' column. 'Runs' says which walk-forward both models of the row come from."
d <- merge(pd[pd$split %in% c("all", "sex", "phase"), ], steps, by = c("variant", "ref"))
cell <- function(m, g) {
  k <- d[d$metric == m & d$group == g, ]
  setNames(paste0(sgn(k$diff), " (", num(k$se, 4), ")"), k$variant)
}
v <- steps$variant[steps$variant %in% d$variant]
tab(data.frame(
  Change = lab(v), Against = lab(steps$ref[match(v, steps$variant)]),
  `1X2, all` = cell("ls_1x2", "all")[v], `Scoreline, all` = cell("ls_score", "all")[v],
  `Scoreline, men` = cell("ls_score", "male")[v], `Scoreline, women` = cell("ls_score", "female")[v],
  `Scoreline, first five rounds` = cell("ls_score", "early")[v], `middle` = cell("ls_score", "middle")[v],
  `last third` = cell("ls_score", "late")[v],
  Runs = d$runs[match(v, d$variant)],
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

### The season break

Two candidates. In both, steps inside a season count weeks as before and the step across seasons becomes its own jump with its own sd $\kappa$.

- **A free break variance** does nothing for the 1X2 score (`r pdv("brk", "base", "ls_1x2")`) and is slightly worse on the scoreline (`r pdv("brk", "base")`). The reference already gives the off-season about 26 weeks of ordinary drift, and the fitted break sd is close to what that implies. Rejected.
- **Reversion.** Teams that stay in their division start the new season part of the way back toward the mean of that division's staying teams: $x_{\text{new}} = m + \rho\,(x_{\text{old}} - m) + \text{jump}$. Teams that are promoted or relegated take a plain jump. With $\rho = 0.8$, fixed in advance from published between-season memory of 0.74 to 0.80, the scoreline score improves by `r pdv("brk_rev80", "base")` and the 1X2 score by `r pdv("brk_rev80", "base", "ls_1x2")`, clearest for men (`r pdv("brk_rev80", "base", "ls_score", "male")`). Kept. Taken out of the recommended model, the last row of @tbl-tests, it costs `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_lvl", "sq_static_lvl")` on the scoreline and `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_lvl", "sq_static_lvl", "ls_1x2")` on the 1X2 score: a smaller effect there than with attack and defence walks, and established on the scoreline only (@sec-rerun).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rho
#| tbl-cap: "The reversion coefficient estimated by NUTS on results to 31 July 2026 (uniform prior on 0 to 1). INLA cannot estimate it: it sits inside the precision matrix. The fits on the recommended model were run again on the code as fixed after the review (@sec-rerun)."
rh <- res$rho
if (!is.null(rh)) {
  r <- rh[rh$parameter == "rho", ]
  form <- c(ad = "Attack and defence walks", final = "Recommended model")
  tab(data.frame(
    Form = form[r$form], ` ` = sex_label[r$sex], `Posterior mean` = num(r$mean, 2),
    `5 % to 95 %` = paste(num(r$q5, 2), "to", num(r$q95, 2)),
    Divergences = r$divergences, `Leapfrogs / iter` = round(r$leapfrog),
    Runs = ifelse(r$rerun, "fixed code", "before the fix"), check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: rho-inline
rh <- res$rho
rho_txt <- function(form, sex) {
  r <- rh[rh$parameter == "rho" & rh$form == form & rh$sex == sex, ]
  if (is.null(rh) || !nrow(r)) "(not run)" else paste0(num(r$mean, 2), " (", num(r$q5, 2), " to ", num(r$q95, 2), ")")
}
```

How strong should the reversion be? INLA has to be told; NUTS can estimate it (@tbl-rho). On the recommended model the posterior mean is `r rho_txt("final", "female")` for women and `r rho_txt("final", "male")` for men; with attack and defence walks it is `r rho_txt("ad", "female")` and `r rho_txt("ad", "male")`. So 0.8 is right for women and on the weak side for men, whose teams give back more of their distance from the division mean over a winter. On the walk-forward the question barely matters: 0.7 instead of 0.8 changes the scoreline score by `r pdv("rev70_sq_static", "rev80_sq_static")` and the 1X2 score by `r pdv("rev70_sq_static", "rev80_sq_static", "ls_1x2")`. The value fixed in advance, 0.8, is kept for the cutover; what matters is that reversion is there, and the Stan reference can refresh the value before each season.

### One strength and a style, or separate attack and defence

Attack and defence can be re-expressed as an overall strength $s$ and a style $q$: attack $= s + q$, defence $= s - q$. Two independent walks of similar volatility for attack and defence amount to assuming that style moves as freely as strength. The alternative puts the dynamics on strength alone and gives each team one fixed style value, shrunk toward zero.

That change is the largest effect found: `r pdv("rev80_sq_static", "brk_rev80", "ls_1x2")` on the 1X2 score and `r pdv("rev80_sq_static", "brk_rev80")` on the scoreline, in both sexes (scoreline: men `r pdv("rev80_sq_static", "brk_rev80", "ls_score", "male")`, women `r pdv("rev80_sq_static", "brk_rev80", "ls_score", "female")`). It is largest early in the season (`r pdv("rev80_sq_static", "brk_rev80", "ls_score", "early")` in the first five rounds), when a team's attack and defence states have each seen few matches and one shared strength uses both its goals scored and its goals conceded. It also halves the number of dynamic states. Kept on both counts.

Is the style term needed at all? Dropping it from the recommended model changes the scoreline score by `r pdv("rev80_sq_none_lvl", "rev80_sq_static_lvl")` and the 1X2 score by `r pdv("rev80_sq_none_lvl", "rev80_sq_static_lvl", "ls_1x2")`. Style does not help say who wins; it helps say how many goals, which is what a side that plays open or closed football should affect. Kept.

**Where the gain comes from, and a result elsewhere that disagrees in size.** A sibling test bed fitted comparable variants to eight large European leagues. Its data may be used for research only, so its figures are not reproduced in this repository; they are in `/Users/brynjolfurjonsson/.claude-reviews/sports-pan-european/structural-tests.md`. In words: strength plus style has the same sign there and a much smaller effect on the 1X2 score, one that cannot be told from zero. Splitting the Icelandic gain shows the two results are closer than they look (@tbl-style-split).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-style-split
#| tbl-cap: "The gain from one strength walk and a fixed style over separate attack and defence walks (both with reversion 0.8), split three ways. Paired differences in log score on the same matches, positive is better, standard errors clustered by fit week in brackets."
ss <- res$style_split
if (!is.null(ss)) {
  tab(data.frame(
    Split = ss$kind, ` ` = ss$group, Matches = format(ss$n, big.mark = ","),
    `1X2 log score` = paste0(sgn(ss$d_1x2), " (", num(ss$se_1x2, 4), ")"),
    `Scoreline log score` = paste0(sgn(ss$d_score), " (", num(ss$se_score, 4), ")"),
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
sp <- function(kind, group, what = "1x2") {
  r <- ss[ss$kind == kind & ss$group == group, ]
  paste0(sgn(r[[paste0("d_", what)]]), " (se ", num(r[[paste0("se_", what)]], 4), ")")
}
sn <- function(kind, group) format(ss$n[ss$kind == kind & ss$group == group], big.mark = ",")
```

- In the **top division** the 1X2 gain is `r sp("Competition", "Top division")` on `r sn("Competition", "Top division")` matches: not distinguishable from zero. That is the closest thing in the Icelandic data to a single top-flight league, and there the two test beds agree.
- The gain sits in the **cup** (`r sp("Competition", "Cup")` on `r sn("Competition", "Cup")` matches) and the **lower divisions** (`r sp("Competition", "Lower divisions")`). Cup ties pair teams from different divisions, and the lower divisions have the thinnest histories. One strength per team is easier to place across divisions than an attack and a defence each.
- It is **largest where the history is shortest**: `r sp("Season", "2022")` in 2022, forecast from one earlier season, and `r sp("Season", "2023")` in 2023, against `r sgn(min(ss$d_1x2[ss$kind == "Season" & ss$group %in% c("2024", "2025", "2026")]))` to `r sgn(max(ss$d_1x2[ss$kind == "Season" & ss$group %in% c("2024", "2025", "2026")]))` in the three seasons since. The decline is not steady from year to year, and each season's standard error is about 0.003.

So the two results agree where they can be compared, and the Icelandic gain comes from what the European test bed does not contain: several divisions joined by a cup, and short histories. That is a breakdown of one experiment, not a new experiment, and three differences between the two set-ups stay untested. The European style term walks, where this one is fixed. Its forecasts run up to six months ahead, where these are a week. And its states follow an autoregression on a four-week grid, where these are a weekly walk with reversion at the break. **Open:** a walk-forward of v2.0 with a walking style term on the Icelandic data, and the fixed-style variant on the European test bed, would settle it. Neither has been run.

### Division structure, and the league's level over time

Tested on the strength-plus-style model, one piece at a time.

- **A promotion and relegation shock** (a mean shift for teams that go up, another for teams that go down, and their own break variance) does nothing: `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_mov", "rev80_sq_static", "ls_1x2")` on the 1X2 score, `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_mov", "rev80_sq_static")` on the scoreline. Teams that change division already take a plain jump instead of reverting, and nothing systematic is left over. Rejected.
- **Division-by-season offsets** for the scoring rate and the home advantage help a little: `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_div", "rev80_sq_static", "ls_1x2")` and `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_div", "rev80_sq_static")`. The reason turned out to matter more than the size.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-goals
#| tbl-cap: "Goals per match on the walk-forward: scored, and predicted by four models. With one strength walk and a fixed style, nothing in the model can follow the league's scoring level; the league-level walks restore that."
gl <- res$goals
if (!is.null(gl)) {
  g <- merge(merge(gl$base[c("sex", "season", "obs", "pred")], gl$sq[c("sex", "season", "pred")], by = c("sex", "season"), suffixes = c("", "_sq")),
    gl$sq_div[c("sex", "season", "pred")], by = c("sex", "season"), suffixes = c("", "_div"))
  if (!is.null(gl$sq_lvl)) g <- merge(g, setNames(gl$sq_lvl[c("sex", "season", "pred")], c("sex", "season", "pred_lvl")), by = c("sex", "season"))
  g <- g[order(g$sex, g$season), ]
  out <- data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[g$sex], Season = g$season, Scored = num(g$obs, 2),
    `Reference (attack and defence walks)` = num(g$pred, 2),
    `Strength + fixed style` = num(g$pred_sq, 2),
    `+ division-by-season offsets` = num(g$pred_div, 2), check.names = FALSE
  )
  if (!is.null(g$pred_lvl)) out$`+ league-level walks` <- num(g$pred_lvl, 2)
  tab(out)
}
```

Two attack and defence walks can absorb a league-wide rise in scoring: every attack drifts up and every defence down. One strength walk with a fixed style cannot, and goals per match rose over these seasons (men: 3.3 in 2021 to 3.9 in 2026). The strength-plus-style model therefore under-predicts goals in the later seasons (@tbl-goals), even while it scores better. Independent division-by-season offsets close part of that gap; they cannot close all of it, because each season's offset starts again from zero.

The repair is to let the league's scoring level, and by the same logic its home advantage, walk over time: two weekly random walks shared by all teams. That is the time-varying form of what this test asked for.

```{r}
#| label: goals-inline
gl <- res$goals
gm <- function(d) if (is.null(d)) NA else mean(d$pred)
```

With the two league-level walks added, predicted goals per match come to `r num(gm(gl$sq_lvl), 2)` (it was `r num(gm(gl$sq), 2)` without them and `r num(gm(gl$sq_div), 2)` with the offsets; `r num(mean(gl$base$obs), 2)` were scored, averaging the sex-season cells), and the scores improve by `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_lvl", "rev80_sq_static", "ls_1x2")` on the 1X2 and `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_lvl", "rev80_sq_static")` on the scoreline.

**Offsets or walks.** On the scores the two are equivalent: the offsets against the walks are `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_div", "rev80_sq_static_lvl", "ls_1x2")` on the 1X2 and `r pdv("rev80_sq_static_div", "rev80_sq_static_lvl")` on the scoreline, and the offsets have the marginally lower 1X2 log loss (`r num(wf$scores$logloss_1x2[wf$scores$variant == "rev80_sq_static_div"], 4)` against `r num(wf$scores$logloss_1x2[wf$scores$variant == "rev80_sq_static_lvl"], 4)`). The walk-forward does not choose between them. I recommend the walks for reasons the scores do not measure: they track the scoring level better (@tbl-goals), because they carry it across the winter where an offset starts again from zero; they need no division labels, which matters for a model meant to be reused across leagues; and they reach the existing season simulators through one number. If you would rather have the offsets, the evidence does not argue against it. The two were not run together.





## Recommended model {#sec-model}

The model that came out of the tests, written out for a match in week $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{home goals} &\sim \text{Poisson}\!\left(\exp\!\left(c_{\text{home}} + g_t + \tfrac12 h_t + (s_{h,t} - s_{w,t}) + (q_h + q_w) + \eta^{a}_{h}\right)\right),\\
\text{away goals} &\sim \text{Poisson}\!\left(\exp\!\left(c_{\text{away}} + g_t - \tfrac12 h_t + (s_{w,t} - s_{h,t}) + (q_h + q_w) - \eta^{d}_{h}\right)\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

- $s_{k,t}$ is team $k$'s **strength** in week $t$: a random walk inside a season (sd $\sigma$ per week), and at the season break a jump (sd $\kappa$) after reverting 20 % of the way to the mean of the division's staying teams. Promoted and relegated teams jump without reverting.
- $q_k$ is a fixed **style** value per team, shrunk toward zero: positive means more goals at both ends than the strengths alone imply.
- $g_t$ and $h_t$ are the **league-wide scoring level and home advantage**, two weekly random walks shared by all teams and centred on zero.
- $c_{\text{home}}, c_{\text{away}}$ and the pooled, sign-free team home-advantage deviations $\eta^a, \eta^d$ are as in the reference specification.
- Eight hyperparameters ($\tau_s, \sigma, \kappa, \tau_q, \omega_a, \omega_d$ and the two league-walk sds) and one fixed constant ($\rho = 0.8$).

Against the reference specification it has half the team-level dynamic states and scores better; against production it removes the home-advantage inflation, the unidentified split, the per-team volatilities, the shared-rate term and the prior-only states.

**This is version 2.0, and it is provisional.** The code names it (`FOOTBALL_V2_VERSION` and `football_v2_options()` in `R/model-v2-fit.R`), and a test checks that those options are the variant this report evaluated. It was chosen on the same `r format(sum(wf$scores_sex$n[wf$scores_sex$variant == wf$ref]), big.mark = ",")` matches it was scored on: each structural test kept what scored better on the walk-forward, and the final score is reported on those same matches. For the two main choices the paired differences are large against their standard errors, but a model picked this way looks better than it is, by an amount this report cannot measure.

::: {.callout-important}
## Follow-up, due 15 July 2027: re-examine v2.0 on matches it has never seen

Using every 2027 match played to 30 June 2027 (about the first half of the league season, and the early cup rounds), repeat the walk-forward for v2.0 and for the alternatives it beat: attack and defence walks with reversion, division offsets in place of the league walks, and the reference specification. Compare with the Stan shadow forecasts and the Lengjan line on the same matches. v2.0 stays if it is not worse than the best alternative by more than one standard error. Otherwise the better model becomes v2.1, and the stored reference of @sec-reftest is regenerated for it.
:::

```{r}
#| label: tbl-model-gain
#| tbl-cap: "The recommended model against the reference specification on the walk-forward (paired, positive is better; standard error in brackets)."
g <- wf$paired[wf$paired$variant == wf$ref & wf$paired$ref == "base" & wf$paired$split %in% c("all", "sex", "phase"), ]
grp <- c(all = "All matches", male = "Men", female = "Women", early = "First five rounds", middle = "Middle", late = "Last third")
w <- reshape(g[c("group", "metric", "diff", "se")], idvar = "group", timevar = "metric", direction = "wide")
tab(data.frame(
  ` ` = grp[w$group], Matches = g$n[match(w$group, g$group)],
  `1X2 log score` = paste0(sgn(w$diff.ls_1x2), " (", num(w$se.ls_1x2, 4), ")"),
  `Scoreline log score` = paste0(sgn(w$diff.ls_score), " (", num(w$se.ls_score, 4), ")"),
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

### Checked against NUTS

The engine gate in @sec-validation was passed on the reference specification. The same check was repeated on the model recommended here, with the reversion coefficient fixed at 0.8 in both engines (NUTS with `adapt_delta` 0.95; INLA's full integration now uses 80 design points for eight hyperparameters).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-final-val
#| tbl-cap: "INLA against NUTS on the recommended model, results to 31 July 2026, held-out matches to 31 October. State and probability differences are for INLA with full integration."
vf <- if (!is.null(res$validation_lvl)) res$validation_lvl else res$validation_sq
if (!is.null(vf)) {
  par_names <- c(
    tau_str = "Entry level sd", sigma_str = "Weekly innovation sd", kappa_str = "Season-break sd",
    tau_sty = "Style sd", omega_att = "Team home-advantage sd, attack", omega_def = "Team home-advantage sd, defence",
    sigma_lvl_goal = "League scoring level, weekly sd", sigma_lvl_ha = "League home advantage, weekly sd"
  )
  h <- vf$hyper
  tab(data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[h$sex], Parameter = par_names[h$parameter],
    `NUTS mean` = num(h$stan_mean, 4), `NUTS 5 % to 95 %` = paste(num(h$stan_q5, 4), "to", num(h$stan_q95, 4)),
    `INLA mean` = num(h$inla_mean, 4), `INLA 5 % to 95 %` = paste(num(h$inla_q5, 4), "to", num(h$inla_q95, 4)),
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-final-val2
#| tbl-cap: "Predictive agreement and sampler effort on the recommended model."
if (!is.null(vf)) {
  ps <- vf$pred_summ
  st <- vf$sampler[vf$sampler$engine == "stan-nuts", ]
  ss <- vf$state_summ[vf$state_summ$engine == "inla-full" & vf$state_summ$has_obs, ]
  rms <- tapply(ss$rms_z, ss$sex, max)
  sc <- vf$scores
  one <- function(sex, eng) sc$logloss_1x2[sc$sex == sex & sc$engine == eng]
  tab(data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[ps$sex], Engine = engine_label[ps$engine], Matches = ps$n,
    `Prob. diff., mean` = num(ps$mean_abs_dp, 4), `largest` = num(ps$max_abs_dp, 4),
    `1X2 log score diff.` = paste0(sgn(ps$d_1x2), " (se ", num(ps$se_1x2, 4), ")"),
    `Scoreline diff.` = paste0(sgn(ps$d_scoreline), " (se ", num(ps$se_scoreline, 4), ")"),
    `State mean RMS diff. (sd)` = num(rms[ps$sex], 3),
    `NUTS leapfrogs / iter` = round(st$leapfrog[match(ps$sex, st$sex)]),
    `NUTS divergences` = st$divergences[match(ps$sex, st$sex)],
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

The recommended model agrees with NUTS as closely as the reference did. The same single departure shows up: where a standard deviation sits near zero (the team home-advantage deviations, the league home-advantage walk, the men's season-break sd) INLA's interval starts higher than NUTS's. Nothing else moves. On the held-out scores INLA's 1X2 log score is below NUTS's in both cells, by `r num(abs(vf$pred_summ$d_1x2[vf$pred_summ$engine == "inla-full" & vf$pred_summ$sex == "female"]), 4)` (se `r num(vf$pred_summ$se_1x2[vf$pred_summ$engine == "inla-full" & vf$pred_summ$sex == "female"], 4)`) for women and `r num(abs(vf$pred_summ$d_1x2[vf$pred_summ$engine == "inla-full" & vf$pred_summ$sex == "male"]), 4)` (se `r num(vf$pred_summ$se_1x2[vf$pred_summ$engine == "inla-full" & vf$pred_summ$sex == "male"], 4)`) for men. Running either engine a second time moves these scores by about as much (@sec-rerun-engine), so neither is a difference between the engines. The scoreline differences are inside one standard error.

**What the fitted values say.** Entry levels are spread about twice as widely for women (sd 0.70) as for men (0.36): the women's divisions are further apart. A team's strength moves about 0.05 a week for women and 0.03 for men inside a season, and jumps by 0.24 and 0.10 across a winter on top of the reversion. Style differences between teams are small (sd 0.07). The league scoring level drifts by just under 0.01 a week, enough to follow the rise in goals; the league home advantage barely moves for men and a little for women.

**Left for later**, none of it needed for the cutover:

- Pass propagated strengths, not current ones, to the season simulators, so season forecasts widen with the horizon as match forecasts already do.
- Let the Stan reference re-estimate the reversion coefficient before each season, and feed INLA the result.
- A low-score dependence term for the women's cell (the literature review's one remaining suggestion for the likelihood).


## Cutover proposal {#sec-cutover}

The owner chose INLA as the production engine on 15 November 2026 and approved this plan on 16 November. Its first two steps are now done on the branch: the engine is in the package (@sec-landed), it runs on a GitHub runner (@sec-runner), and a set of 2026 dates has been replayed against what production published (@sec-replay). The switch is not done. `config/leagues.yml`, `Stan/` and every workflow that runs on `main` are unchanged.

### What the existing layers need from a fit

The extract, publish and simulation layers touch a fit through one method, `fit$draws(name)`, and expect the production Stan program's variable names. That makes the cutover an adapter problem, not a rewrite. The adapter (`R/model-v2-adapter.R`, `fv2_as_fit()`) presents the new engine's draws under those names:

| Production name | From the new model |
|---|---|
| `mean_log_goals` | $(c_{\text{home}} + c_{\text{away}})/2$, plus the league scoring level of the first fixture week |
| `home_advantage_off[k]`, `home_advantage_def[k]` | $(c_{\text{home}} - c_{\text{away}})/2 + \eta^a_k$ and $\ldots + \eta^d_k$ |
| `home_advantage_tot[k]` | their sum |
| `cur_offense_away[k]`, `cur_defense_away[k]` and the `_home` and `cur_strength_*` variants | the state at team $k$'s next match (its first fixture, or the start of the season being forecast), or at its last match when no later one is known; plus home advantage |
| `offense[r, k]`, `defense[r, k]` | the weekly state in the week of team $k$'s $r$-th match |
| `alpha_mu3`, `beta_mu3_strength_diff` | a large negative constant and zero: the shared-rate term is switched off |
| `goals1_pred[n]`, `goals2_pred[n]` | Poisson counts drawn from the predictive rates of fixture $n$, which already carry the forward propagation |
| `lp__` | a placeholder; only the number of draws is read from it |

A unit test runs production's own `extract_posteriors()` on an adapted fit.

**Dry run.** The whole chain was run on real data for two dates, writing only to an isolated tree outside the repository: production's `prepare_data()`, an INLA fit of the recommended model, the adapter, then production's unchanged `extract_football_iceland()` and `publish_iceland_league()`.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dry
#| tbl-cap: "End-to-end dry runs of the cutover path. Schema validation is production's own `validate_publish_dir()`; one file per run (the cup `bracket.json`) has no schema to check against. The last columns compare the new model's home-win probabilities with production's stored extract for the same fit date."
if (!is.null(dr)) {
  d <- list(dm, dw)
  f <- function(k) vapply(d, function(x) as.character(x[[k]]), character(1))
  tab(data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[f("sex")], `As of` = f("as_of"),
    `Extract files` = f("extract_files"), `JSON files` = f("n_json"),
    `Validated against a schema` = vapply(d, function(x) paste0(x$schema$n_passed, " of ", x$schema$n_files), character(1)),
    `Fixtures compared` = f("fixtures"),
    `Mean P(home): new / production` = vapply(d, function(x) paste(num(x$p_home_v2, 3), num(x$p_home_prod, 3), sep = " / "), character(1)),
    `Mean abs. difference` = vapply(d, function(x) num(x$mean_abs_dp, 3), character(1)),
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

Every extract file production writes was written, every published JSON that has a schema passed it, and nothing under `data/` changed (`git status` clean afterwards). The INLA fit with 2,000 posterior draws took about 20 seconds in each run; the step that dominates is the existing per-draw season simulation inside the extract (77 and 130 seconds), which the cutover does not touch.

Three things change in meaning and should be known before the first published fit:

- **Home advantage split.** The league home advantage is divided evenly between "attack" and "defence", because only its total is identified. The published attack and defence home-advantage numbers become a presentation convention; the total is the estimate.
- **Strengths in the season simulation.** The simulators hold each team's strength at one value for all remaining matches, as they do today. On this engine that value is the team's state at its *next* match, the same state the forecast of that match uses, so the two never disagree about what lies between the last result and the next match: a week of drift in season, the whole season break before one. Before a season every team the schedule lists is carried across the break, including those whose first match is beyond the fit horizon, so a simulated table never mixes teams that have reverted toward their division mean with teams that have not. Forecasts of later matches still widen with the horizon and the simulation does not; passing per-fixture states to the simulators is a follow-up.
- **Trajectory.** The published strength trajectory stays indexed by a team's match count. Two matches in one week now share a state.

### What has landed {#sec-landed}

| File | What it does now |
|---|---|
| `config/leagues.schema.json` | Optional league key `engine`, `stan` or `inla`; absent means `stan`. `config/leagues.yml` is unchanged, so no league sets it. `stan_model` stays required. |
| `R/model-v2-spec.R` | The specification: build, precision pieces, design, Stan data, prediction. |
| `R/model-v2-inla.R` | The INLA engine, and the check that INLA used the priors it was given. |
| `R/model-v2-adapter.R` | `fv2_as_fit()`: the draws under production's variable names. |
| `R/model-v2-fit.R` | The version and options of v2.0; `fit_model_v2_inla()`, which takes its training rows from `model_training_results()` and its fixtures from `prepare_data()` and returns the adapted fit; the gate; the diagnostics row. |
| `R/model-league.R` | `fit_league()` picks the engine from `league$engine`. The Stan branch is the call it made before, with the same arguments. `run_fit_targets()` keeps `engine` in the slice of the league it hands on (the trap that once dropped `training_filter`). |
| `R/model-prepare.R`, `R/model-fit.R`, extract, publish, simulators, decide | No change. |
| `Stan/` | No change. The reference program stays at `research/football-v2/stan/fv2_rev.stan` until the switch, when it moves to `Stan/football_iceland/` for the weekly reference fit. |
| `DESCRIPTION` | `Matrix` under `Imports`, the new files in `Collate`. INLA is not declared; see below. |

**The gate for INLA fits.** `check_stan_diagnostics()` aborts when it is handed anything that is not a cmdstanr fit, and its checks (divergences, $\hat{R}$, ESS, tree depth, E-BFMI) have no INLA counterpart. `fv2_inla_gate()` checks what can go wrong with an INLA fit instead, and a breach stops the fit before anything is extracted:

1. the hyperparameter mode was found (`mode.status` is 0);
2. every sd is inside a plausible range, so a run-away precision is caught (the home-advantage sds are the ones at risk);
3. no posterior draw is `NA` or infinite, and the entry levels sum to zero, which is the model's identification;
4. the mean predicted goals per match sit in a sane band;
5. hyperparameters have not moved from the previous fit by more than a set factor.

An INLA fit also writes a row to the `fit_diagnostics` store, with the number of training matches and `NA` for the sampler metrics (the health check reads `NA` as nothing to report). `needs_refit()` reads the match count off the newest row, so without it an old Stan row would stay "latest" for the cell.

**Where this departs from the plan as first written.**

- **INLA is not in `DESCRIPTION` yet.** The decision is `Suggests`. But `fit`, `decide-publish`, `republish` and `world-cup` install every suggested package, so declaring INLA now would make four workflows on `main` install it, with its repository and the system libraries of @sec-runner, before any league uses it. This step was told to leave the scheduled workflows alone, so the declaration goes with the switch. Until then the code guards with `requireNamespace()` and stops with an instruction if a league asks for INLA where it is absent.
- **The rule for short histories is a count of earlier seasons.** The owner's rule is that a league with only one season of history stays on Stan. In code, the INLA engine refuses a cell with fewer than two seasons of results before the season being forecast. The regime that failed (@sec-accept) has one: a complete season, and the first weeks of the next. Counting against the season of the fixtures, not the calendar, gives the same answer before a season starts and a month into it. Nothing between one earlier season and five was tested, so two is where the evidence stops being bad, not where it has been shown to be good.
