- **The gate's fifth check needs a previous fit, and says so when there is none.** Each INLA fit records its hyperparameters in the diagnostics store, which the fit workflow commits, and the next fit of the cell is compared with them: a move by more than a factor 3 either way is refused (over 70 consecutive re-estimates of each hyperparameter in the walk-forward the largest move was a factor 1.65). The first INLA fit of a cell has nothing to be compared with. `fit_league()` then says in the log that the check will not run and the stored row records it, so a check that did not run is never reported as passed. A refused change that turns out to be real can be accepted by the operator (`SPORTS_INLA_ACCEPT_JUMP=1`).
- **An independent review of the change found three things, all fixed.** The gate's first check skipped when INLA returned an empty mode status, where it must fail. A fit with no fixture left to predict, which a round-by-round replay reaches at the end of a season, stopped in the adapter. And the short-history rule as first written counted the season in progress, so the same history passed in May and failed in February.
- **Divisions come from the schedule, not only from results.** The season-break step needs to know which division a team plays in next season. A team with no division for the new season is treated as having stayed, and reverts toward the wrong division's mean. So the division table is built from every known match of a season, played or scheduled. Which division a club is in is public before the first match, and no score enters it.

**Tests.** `tests/testthat/test-model-v2.R` covers the specification, the adapter, the gate, the engine choice in `fit_league()` (Stan unless the league says otherwise; an unknown engine is an error), the diagnostics row, and an end-to-end INLA fit of a small store read by production's `extract_posteriors()`. R-INLA reruns are not guaranteed to be bit-identical, so that test fixes the seed and the threads and compares a rerun at a tolerance. One test pins that no league is on the INLA engine, so the switch has to edit an expectation; another checks that the options the package fits are the variant this report evaluated. The engine tests skip where INLA is not installed, which today includes `ci-tests.yml`; the INLA workflow runs them with INLA present and treats a missing INLA as a failure.

### What an independent review of the pull request found {#sec-review}

The owner had the pull request reviewed by a session that had not written it. It found nine defects. A second reviewer traced each one in the code and confirmed all nine. None is on the `engine: stan` path, so nothing that runs today was wrong; all of them would have mattered at the switch. Each was fixed test-first: the test was written, seen to fail for the stated reason, and only then made to pass.

| | What was wrong | What changed | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The mean a staying team reverts toward at the season break was taken over the stayers that already had a slot in the new season. Early in a season a team whose division mates had not played yet was alone in its group, and reverting toward yourself is a plain jump: the fixed $\rho = 0.8$ silently became 1. | `fv2_reversion_groups()` defines the group once: every team that stays in the division, with a new-season slot or without. | "a stayer reverts toward all of its division's stayers, slot in the new season or not" |
| 2 | The two tests of the reversion used a league with a single stayer, so $\rho$ had no effect in them. They passed with the reversion switched off. | Tests on leagues of three and four stayers; one compares the prior with the covariance written out from the model, not from the package. With the precision made to ignore $\rho$ the old tests pass and the new ones fail. | "reversion pulls every stayer toward the mean of its division's stayers"; "the reverting break is the same prior in INLA's and Stan's form" |
| 3 | The simulators were handed each team's state at its last result; the forecast of a fixture uses the state at the fixture. Before a season the forecast had crossed the break and the season and cup simulations of the same match had not. | "Current" now means "at the team's next match", for states and for league levels. Teams whose first match is beyond the horizon are carried across the break. | "the simulators and the forecast give a team's next match the same rates"; "across a season break the simulators see what the forecast sees" |
| 4 | After a merge nothing would have run the tests that fit with INLA: they skip in `ci-tests.yml`, and the trial ran only for this branch. | `inla-engine.yml` runs them on pull requests that touch the package, and weekly; there a missing INLA fails instead of skipping. | `test-workflow-inla-engine.R` |
| 5 | The Stan data averaged a reversion group within the season the breaks arrive in, INLA within the season they leave. The two engines disagreed when a team sat out a season. | Both read the one definition of finding 1; the Stan program takes the members as data. | "INLA's and Stan's forms agree when a team sits out a season"; the compiled Stan recursion against its R twin |
| 6 | The seed did not make an INLA fit reproducible under full integration: INLA assigns draws to hyperparameter configurations with R's generator, which nothing seeded. | R's generator is seeded for the sampling call. | "the seed fixes an INLA fit's draws, whatever R's own generator is doing" |
| 7 | The gate's hyperparameter-jump check never ran in production, because no previous fit's values were kept; the gate reported a pass regardless. | Hyperparameters are stored with each fit and read back for the next; when there are none the log and the stored row say the check did not run. | "a real INLA fit through fit_league is checked against the fit before it", and two more |
| 8 | An INLA fit's provenance row in the permanent extracts named the league's Stan file. | The row names the engine and the model version; older partitions and Stan fits read as `stan`. | "an INLA fit's fit_meta names the engine and the model, not a Stan file" |
| 9 | `engine: inla` loaded for handball and basketball, and would then have aborted at every nightly fit. | The config schema refuses it for any sport but football. | "load_leagues() refuses engine: inla for a league that is not football" |

Findings 1 and 5 are the same question answered twice: who stays in a division, and so whose end-of-season state is in the mean. The answer now lives in one function that both engines read. A team stays in division $d$ after season $t$ when the schedule lists it in $d$ for $t+1$. While nothing is listed yet for $d$ in $t+1$, every team of $d$ counts as staying. Once the division's next season is listed, a team absent from it has left, takes a plain jump and is not in the mean.

**What the fixes do to the evidence in this report.** Findings 1 and 5 change which model is fitted whenever a division's staying teams have not all played in the new season, or a team has left or sat out a season. Finding 3 changes what the simulators are handed. So the evidence the recommendation rests on was run again on the fixed code, and @sec-rerun sets each old value beside the new one. No comparison there moves by more than `r num(max(abs(rr$headline$new - rr$headline$old) / rr$headline$new_se), 1)` of its standard error.

- **The walk-forward** was re-run for the recommended model, the reference and the two models that bracket the reversion (@sec-rerun).
- **The engine comparison with NUTS** was re-run at all three cutoffs, because the corrected groups reach the fits that were validated (@sec-rerun-engine).
- **The replay** (@sec-replay) was re-run after all nine fixes. Finding 3 changes what an INLA fit publishes as a team's current strength and what the season simulation starts from, most of all before a season.
- **The runner.** The real-data fits on a GitHub runner (@sec-runner) predate the fixes. Since then the runner has run the engine tests on every push, which include real INLA fits through `fit_league()` on a small store, but not the two football cells again.

**The fixes were checked by a session that did not write them.** It ran each test at the fixed commit, undid each fix and saw the test fail, and looked for new defects in the ten commits. Its log is the last entry of `/Users/brynjolfurjonsson/.claude-reviews/sports-model-research-2026-11-15/ORCHESTRATION.md`; a second, separate re-run of five of the failure proofs is in `spot_red.log` in the same folder.

### The evidence re-run on the fixed code {#sec-rerun}

```{r}
#| label: review-evidence
sc <- gs$scan
sc_all <- sum(sc$n_pred)
sc_hit <- sum(sc$n_pred[sc$differing > 0])
sc_new <- sum(sc$n_pred[sc$differing_newest > 0])
sc_old <- sum(sc$n_pred[sc$differing_newest == 0 & sc$differing_older > 0])
hl <- rr$headline
hrow <- function(pattern, metric) hl[grepl(pattern, hl$comparison) & hl$metric == metric, ]
est <- function(x, se) paste0(sgn(x), " (", num(se, 4), ")")
# A change too small for four decimals is shown as zero, not as a signed zero.
est0 <- function(x, se) ifelse(abs(x) < 5e-5 & se < 5e-5, "0.0000", est(x, se))
mv <- rr$move_all
mrec <- mv[mv$variant == wf$ref, ]
mbase <- mv[mv$variant == "base", ]
mp <- rr$move_prior[rr$move_prior$variant == wf$ref, ]
big <- rr$largest[1, ]
pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(num(100 * x, d), " %")
stale <- setdiff(ladder$scores$variant[grepl("rev[0-9]", ladder$scores$variant)], rerun_set)
```

**How much of the walk-forward the fix reaches.** Rebuilding the specification at every one of the `r nrow(sc)` weekly cutoffs (no model fitted) shows that `r format(sc_hit, big.mark = ",")` of the `r format(sc_all, big.mark = ",")` forecasts (`r num(100 * sc_hit / sc_all, 1)` %) come from a fit whose prior differs at all under the corrected definition. `r format(sc_new, big.mark = ",")` of those are the early-season case of finding 1, where not every staying team had a slot in the new season yet; the other `r format(sc_old, big.mark = ",")` differ only at an older break, through a team that left or sat out a season. Those fits had run under a prior with less reversion than intended.

**What was run again.** The same weekly cutoffs, seeds and settings, on the fixed code, for four models: the recommended model, the reference specification, the recommended model with the reversion taken out, and attack and defence walks with reversion 0.8 (the model behind the first reversion test in @sec-tests). The model without the reversion had not been run before. It has no reversion groups, so it is the same model on either side of the fix.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rerun
#| tbl-cap: "The comparisons the choice of model rests on, from the walk-forward before the fix and from the re-run on the fixed code. Paired log-score differences on the same matches, positive when the first model named scores better; standard error in brackets. In the fourth row the model without reversion is the run from before in both columns (no reversion, so nothing to fix); in the fifth and sixth it is the run on the fixed code in both columns."
short <- c(
  "Recommended model against the reference", "Recommended model against the reference",
  "Reversion 0.8 against none: attack and defence walks, against the reference",
  "Reversion 0.8 against none: attack and defence walks, both with the season-break step",
  "Reversion 0.8 against none: inside the recommended model", "Reversion 0.8 against none: inside the recommended model",
  "Recommended model against production's last forecast, priced matches 2026",
  "Recommended model against production's pre-round forecast, 2026",
  "Recommended model against the Lengjan line, priced matches 2026"
)
stopifnot(nrow(hl) == length(short))
tab(data.frame(
  Comparison = short, Score = ifelse(hl$metric == "1X2", "1X2", "Scoreline"), Matches = format(hl$n, big.mark = ","),
  `Before the fix` = est(hl$old, hl$old_se), `Fixed code` = est(hl$new, hl$new_se),
  Change = sgn(hl$new - hl$old),
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

- **The margin over the reference is unchanged**: `r est(hrow("^Recommended against the reference", "scoreline")$new, hrow("^Recommended against the reference", "scoreline")$new_se)` on the scoreline and `r est(hrow("^Recommended against the reference", "1X2")$new, hrow("^Recommended against the reference", "1X2")$new_se)` on the 1X2 score, five to six standard errors each.
- **The reversion keeps its place, and its size is now measured directly.** The owner's figure for it, attack and defence walks with reversion against the reference, is `r est(hrow("walks against the reference$", "scoreline")$new, hrow("walks against the reference$", "scoreline")$new_se)` on the fixed code. The new run asks the question of the recommended model itself: with the reversion it scores `r est(hrow("in the recommended model", "scoreline")$new, hrow("in the recommended model", "scoreline")$new_se)` better on the scoreline and `r est(hrow("in the recommended model", "1X2")$new, hrow("in the recommended model", "1X2")$new_se)` better on the 1X2 score than without it. That is `r num(hrow("in the recommended model", "scoreline")$new / hrow("in the recommended model", "scoreline")$new_se, 1)` standard errors on the scoreline and `r num(hrow("in the recommended model", "1X2")$new / hrow("in the recommended model", "1X2")$new_se, 1)` on the 1X2: established on the measure used for model development, not on the 1X2 alone, which is where the style term stands too. It is a small effect, about a twelfth of the model's margin over the reference.
- **Against production and the line** the 2026 comparisons move in the fourth decimal.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rerun-moves
#| tbl-cap: "How far the forecasts of one model moved between the walk-forward before the fix and the re-run. A forecast is one match; its move is the largest change among its three outcome probabilities. The last two columns are the model's own log scores, re-run minus before, with week-clustered standard errors. The reference has no reversion, so its row is the size of re-run noise."
prior_label <- c(
  unchanged = "from fits the fix does not reach", `older break only` = "from fits it reaches at an older break only",
  `newest break` = "from fits it reaches at the newest break"
)
mp <- mp[match(names(prior_label), mp$prior), ]
rows <- rbind(
  cbind(what = "Recommended model, all forecasts", mrec[setdiff(names(mrec), "variant")]),
  cbind(what = paste("Recommended model,", prior_label[as.character(mp$prior)]), mp[setdiff(names(mp), c("variant", "prior"))]),
  cbind(what = "Reference, all forecasts", mbase[setdiff(names(mbase), "variant")])
)
tab(data.frame(
  ` ` = rows$what, Forecasts = format(rows$n, big.mark = ","),
  `Mean move` = num(rows$mean_move, 4), `99th percentile` = num(rows$q99_move, 4), Largest = num(rows$max_move, 4),
  `Moved by more than 0.01` = pct(rows$share_over_001), `by more than 0.02` = pct(rows$share_over_002),
  `Scoreline, change` = est0(rows$d_score, rows$d_score_se), `1X2, change` = est0(rows$d_1x2, rows$d_1x2_se),
  check.names = FALSE
))
```

- **The largest change in any single match probability is `r num(mrec$max_move, 3)`** (`r if (big$sex == "female") "women" else "men"`, `r big$home_team` against `r big$away_team`, `r format(as.Date(big$match_date), "%e %B %Y")`: home win `r num(big$p_home_old, 3)` before, `r num(big$p_home_new, 3)` after). **`r pct(mrec$share_over_001)` of the forecasts moved by more than 0.01**, `r pct(mrec$share_over_002)` by more than 0.02 and none by more than 0.05.
- **The scan and the re-run agree on which fits changed.** Forecasts from fits the scan calls unchanged moved by at most `r num(mp$max_move[mp$prior == "unchanged"], 4)`, and the reference by at most `r formatC(mbase$max_move, format = "f", digits = 5)`: re-run noise is negligible, so the moves in the other rows are the fix.
- **Where the fix bites, the corrected model scores a little worse than the uncorrected one**, `r est(mp$d_score[mp$prior == "newest break"], mp$d_score_se[mp$prior == "newest break"])` on the scoreline in the newest-break fits. That is `r num(abs(mp$d_score[mp$prior == "newest break"]) / mp$d_score_se[mp$prior == "newest break"], 1)` standard errors, so it is not evidence against the correction, but it fits the picture of a reversion that helps a little, not a lot.

**The recommendation stands.** The margin over the reference did not shrink, and the reversion still earns its place on the scoreline. Nothing in the specification was changed. For completeness, the alternative the new run prices: the recommended model without the reversion gives up `r num(hrow("in the recommended model", "scoreline")$new, 4)` on the scoreline and `r num(hrow("in the recommended model", "1X2")$new, 4)` on the 1X2 score, has no reversion groups at all (the part of the code findings 1 and 5 were in) and needs no fixed $\rho$. I would keep the reversion: its gain has the same sign for men and women and in every season phase on the scoreline, and NUTS, which can estimate $\rho$, puts it well below one (@tbl-rho).

**What was not re-run.** The other `r length(stale)` models of the selection ladder that have a reversion are as fitted before the fix (marked in @tbl-wf-models and @tbl-tests). The two reversion models that were re-run moved their paired comparisons by at most `r num(max(abs(hl$new - hl$old)[1:6]), 4)`, against ladder steps of 0.003 to 0.02, so the order of the ladder is not in question. Running them again would be `r 10 * length(stale)` walk-forward jobs, one per model, sex and season.

### The engine comparison on the fixed code {#sec-rerun-engine}

```{r}
#| label: tbl-rerun-engine
#| tbl-cap: "INLA with full integration against NUTS on the recommended model, before the fix and on the fixed code, on held-out matches. 'Breaks changed' is how many season-break steps of the fit differ under the corrected reversion groups. Probability columns are absolute differences in the three outcome probabilities, mean and largest. 'NUTS twice' and 'INLA twice' compare the run before the fix with the run after it for one engine: where no break changed that is two runs of one model, so it is the size of Monte Carlo noise. Scoreline columns are differences in the mean held-out log score."
en <- res$engine_noise
if (!is.null(en)) {
  setting <- c(finallvl = "Late July 2026 (main check)", early26 = "Early 2026", early22 = "Early 2022, one season of data")
  two <- function(a, b, d = 4) paste(num(a, d), "/", num(b, d))
  tab(data.frame(
    Setting = setting[en$tag], ` ` = sex_label[en$sex], Matches = en$matches,
    `Breaks changed` = paste(en$breaks_changed, "of", en$breaks),
    `INLA against NUTS, before: mean / largest` = two(en$before_mean, en$before_max),
    `fixed code: mean / largest` = two(en$after_mean, en$after_max),
    `NUTS twice: mean / largest` = two(en$nuts_rerun_mean, en$nuts_rerun_max),
    `INLA twice: mean / largest` = two(en$inla_rerun_mean, en$inla_rerun_max),
    `Scoreline, INLA minus NUTS: before / fixed` = paste(sgn(en$before_scoreline), "/", sgn(en$after_scoreline)),
    `NUTS twice / INLA twice` = paste(sgn(en$nuts_rerun_scoreline), "/", sgn(en$inla_rerun_scoreline)),
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: rerun-engine-inline
same <- en[en$breaks_changed == 0, ]
hist5 <- en[en$tag != "early22", ]
one <- en[en$tag == "early22", ]
nuts_ok <- do.call(rbind, lapply(list(res$validation_lvl, res$validation_early26, res$validation_early22), function(v) v$sampler[v$sampler$engine == "stan-nuts", ]))
w26 <- en[en$tag == "early26" & en$sex == "female", ]
w22 <- en[en$tag == "early22" & en$sex == "female", ]
```

The corrected groups reach four of the six fits that had been compared with NUTS, so all six were run again: NUTS with the same seed and settings, INLA in both modes. The six NUTS fits ran with `r sum(nuts_ok$divergences)` divergences and a largest state Rhat of `r num(max(nuts_ok$max_rhat), 3)`.

- **The table needs its two "twice" columns to be read.** At the women's early-2026 cutoff no break changed and INLA found the same mode to four decimals, so the model fitted before and after is the same. Two NUTS runs of it still differ by `r num(w26$nuts_rerun_mean, 4)` on average and by up to `r num(w26$nuts_rerun_max, 3)` on a single match, and their held-out scoreline scores differ by `r num(abs(w26$nuts_rerun_scoreline), 3)`. (The fix changed the arithmetic of the Stan program, so the same seed gives different draws.) Two sets of INLA draws from the one fit differ by as much.
- **With five seasons of data the engines agree to within what 4,000 draws can resolve, before the fix and after.** INLA differs from NUTS by `r rng(hist5$after_mean, 3)` on average and by `r rng(hist5$after_max, 3)` at most on the fixed code; one engine run twice differs by `r rng(c(hist5$nuts_rerun_mean, hist5$inla_rerun_mean), 3)` on average and up to `r num(max(c(hist5$nuts_rerun_max, hist5$inla_rerun_max)), 3)`. The differences in held-out score between the engines are likewise the size of the differences between two runs of one engine. So the small shifts between the "before" and "fixed code" columns are Monte Carlo noise, not the fix.
- **With one season of data the difference between the engines is real, as before.** At the 2022 cutoff INLA differs from NUTS by `r rng(one$after_mean, 3)` on average, two to three times the rerun noise, and its scoreline score is lower by `r rng(abs(one$after_scoreline), 3)` (it was `r rng(abs(one$before_scoreline), 3)` before the fix). The rule that such a cell stays on Stan stands.
- **Full integration on one season of data is not stable from run to run.** At the women's 2022 cutoff, where the model did not change, the second run placed 77 integration points where the first placed 67, and the posterior means of the two team home-advantage sds came out 28 % lower. The match probabilities of the two runs still agree to `r num(w22$inla_rerun_mean, 3)` on average. With five seasons the two runs found the same mode and the same hyperparameter summaries.

**The other checks of the recommended model were run again as well.**

```{r}
#| label: rerun-other
rho_of <- function(d, sex) {
  x <- d[d$parameter == "rho" & d$form == "final" & d$sex == sex, ]
  paste0(num(x$mean, 2), " (", num(x$q5, 2), " to ", num(x$q95, 2), ")")
}
nr_before <- if (length(res$simcheck_before) == 2) unlist(lapply(c("INLA full against NUTS", "INLA empirical Bayes against NUTS"), function(comparison) {
  vapply(res$simcheck_before, function(z) {
    z <- z[z$outcome == "all places", ]
    (z$mean_abs[z$comparison == comparison] / z$mean_abs[z$comparison == "NUTS half against NUTS half"]) / sqrt(1.5 / 2)
  }, numeric(1))
})) else NA
```

- **The reversion coefficient estimated by NUTS** (@tbl-rho) is `r rho_of(res$rho, "female")` for women and `r rho_of(res$rho, "male")` for men on the fixed code; it was `r rho_of(res$rho_before, "female")` and `r rho_of(res$rho_before, "male")`. The same fit with attack and defence walks was not run again.
- **Season-simulation agreement** (criterion (c) in @sec-accept): INLA against NUTS is at `r rng(nr, 2)` times the pure-noise level, where it was `r rng(nr_before, 2)`. This is also the check of finding 3, because the season simulation now starts from each team's state at its next match.
- **Weekly against four-weekly re-estimation of the hyperparameters** (@sec-limits) gives the same differences as before.
- **The replay** of six 2026 dates (@sec-replay) was run again; its numbers below are from the fixed code.

### CI

- **Installing INLA.** INLA is not on CRAN. What the INLA workflow does, and what works (@sec-runner): install the system libraries by hand, let `setup-r-dependencies` install INLA's R dependencies and the `sn` package, then install INLA's tarball by name from its own repository, which is also the version pin. INLA lists `sn` only as a suggestion, but its posterior sampler stops without it; the first run on the runner failed on exactly that, and the engine now names both packages when either is missing. The system libraries are needed because INLA imports `fmesher`, which imports `sf`, whose binary loads GDAL, GEOS, PROJ and udunits, and the workflows here turn off automatic system requirements (`PKG_SYSREQS: "false"`). `fit.yml` needs these steps at the switch; the workflows that never fit need them only because they install suggested packages.
- **Where to declare it.** Decided: under `Suggests`, with the install steps added to the four workflows that install all suggested packages (`fit`, `decide-publish`, `republish`, `world-cup`), in the same PR as the switch. No test reads `DESCRIPTION` and no workflow runs `R CMD check`, so until then the undeclared, guarded `INLA::` calls fail only where a league asks for INLA and the package is absent.
- **Pin the version.** The trial installs 25.06.07, the version every number in this report was measured with. INLA's repository keeps one tarball per release, so the pin is a file name. Cache the R library at the switch, as the CmdStan install is cached today.
- **CmdStan.** The reference program compiles under 2.38.0, the version `fit.yml` and `ci-tests.yml` pin, and under 2.40.0, the local default (both checked). The pin stays necessary for handball, basketball and the reference check. Moving CI to 2.40.0 is a separate, small PR; it should not ride with the engine change.
- **Tests.** The engine tests skip in `ci-tests.yml`, where INLA is absent. They run in their own workflow, `.github/workflows/inla-engine.yml`: on every pull request to `main` that touches the package, its tests or its config, once a week, and by hand. There a test that needs INLA fails when INLA is missing instead of skipping, and the workflow runs every test file that fits with INLA, found by search and not listed. It is read-only and creates nothing in the repository. The weekly run is there because a moved runner image or a changed INLA repository breaks an engine nobody touched; it is one line to remove if the owner does not want a scheduled job for an engine not yet in use.
- **Run time.** `fit.yml`'s 360-minute timeout is pinned by a test. It can come down once football no longer needs NUTS, but not in the cutover PR.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-timing
#| tbl-cap: "Fitting the recommended model to results up to 31 July 2026 on this Mac (M1 Pro, 8 performance cores), four cores per engine, one engine at a time, with no other model fit running (all three compute slots free at the start and at the end). The machine was not idle: two macOS sync daemons were using about 2.5 cores, which is the load average shown. INLA's totals include drawing 1,000 posterior samples; NUTS's include reading 4,000 draws back."
tm <- res$timing
if (!is.null(tm)) {
  t <- tm$timing
  tab(data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[t$sex], Engine = engine_label[ifelse(t$engine == "inla-auto", "inla-full", t$engine)],
    `Fit, wall s` = num(t$fit_secs, 0), `Fit + draws, wall s` = num(t$total_wall, 0),
    `CPU s` = num(t$cpu_secs, 0), `Load average before` = num(t$load_before, 0),
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: timing-inline
tt <- res$timing$timing
cpu_ratio <- function(sex) {
  if (is.null(tt)) return("(not timed)")
  num(tt$cpu_secs[tt$sex == sex & tt$engine == "stan-nuts"] / tt$cpu_secs[tt$sex == sex & tt$engine == "inla-eb"], 0)
}
```

In CPU time, INLA with empirical Bayes costs `r cpu_ratio("female")` times less than NUTS for the women's cell and `r cpu_ratio("male")` times less for the men's. For scale, the pilot measured production's NUTS fits at 19.6 and 28.2 minutes of wall-clock on this machine (under load). GitHub's runners were not timed.

### INLA on a GitHub runner {#sec-runner}

Whether INLA would install and fit on a GitHub runner was the one thing the first version of this report could not show. A workflow that ran for this branch only ("INLA Engine Trial") showed it; the table below is one of its runs. It had read-only permissions, wrote outside the checkout, uploaded its output as an artifact and created no commit. After the review (@sec-review) that workflow became the permanent `.github/workflows/inla-engine.yml`, which runs the engine tests on pull requests and weekly, and makes the two real-data fits below only when started by hand with `replay: true`.

```{r}
#| label: runner-data
trial_files <- file.path("2026-11-15-football-v2", sprintf("runner-trial-%s.json", c("male", "female")))
trial <- if (all(file.exists(trial_files))) lapply(trial_files, jsonlite::fromJSON)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-runner
#| tbl-cap: "The trial on a GitHub-hosted runner: workflow run 43853199174 on commit `ce86f25c9`, `ubuntu-latest` (Ubuntu 26.04, four cores), R 4.5.3, INLA 25.06.07, full integration, 4,000 draws. `fit_league()` includes production's per-draw season simulation, which is the same code whichever engine made the draws. Wall-clock seconds on a shared runner, for scale only."
if (!is.null(trial)) {
  f <- function(g) vapply(trial, g, character(1))
  tab(data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[f(function(x) x$sex)], `As of` = f(function(x) x$as_of),
    `Matches the fit saw` = f(function(x) format(x$fit$n_obs, big.mark = ",")),
    `Production's fit saw` = f(function(x) format(x$production_n_obs, big.mark = ",")),
    `INLA fit, s` = f(function(x) num(x$fit$seconds$fit, 0)),
    `4,000 draws, s` = f(function(x) num(x$fit$seconds$draws, 0)),
    `fit_league(), s` = f(function(x) num(x$timing$fit_league$elapsed, 0)),
    `Publish, s` = f(function(x) num(x$timing$publish$elapsed, 0)),
    `JSON files` = f(function(x) as.character(x$json_files)),
    `Schema-valid` = f(function(x) paste0(x$schema$n_passed, " of ", x$schema$n_passed + x$schema$n_failed)),
    Gate = f(function(x) if (isTRUE(x$fit$gate$passed)) "passed" else "failed"),
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

What the trial did, in order, and what each step established:

1. **Installs the system libraries `sf` loads** (GDAL, GEOS, PROJ, udunits) with `apt-get`. INLA imports `fmesher`, which imports `sf`, and the workflows here switch off automatic system requirements.
2. **Installs INLA's R dependencies and `sn`**, then **INLA 25.06.07** from its tarball in INLA's own repository. The binaries bundled in that tarball run on the runner image as they are; no separate binary install was needed.
3. **Fits a trivial model** with INLA, to separate "INLA does not run here" from anything about this package.
4. **Runs the engine tests with INLA present**, where a skipped test counts as a failure.
5. **Fits each football cell through `fit_league()`** with `engine: inla` set on the league in memory, then runs production's extract and publish code and validates every published file against its schema (@tbl-runner).
6. **Checks that nothing under `data/` changed.**

The runner image matters here, and it changed during this work's lifetime: `ubuntu-latest` became Ubuntu 26.04 on 12 November 2026. The trial ran on the new image, so the table above is for the image production will use. The same change of image broke the Stan side, which has nothing to do with INLA but showed up in this pull request's tests: the CmdStan cache key said only `ubuntu-latest`, so a toolchain built on the old image was restored on the new one and every compiled chain aborted. Naming the image in the key fixed it: on this branch, changing only that key took the tests from two failing Stan tests to none (workflow run 43858800672), which is what proved the cause. The fix for all three workflows that share the key (`ci-tests.yml`, `fit.yml`, `world-cup.yml`) was made separately, in [metill-is/sports#106](https://github.com/metill-is/sports/pull/106), merged on 16 November 2026. This branch has `main` merged in and no longer differs from it in any existing workflow.

Two things went wrong on the way, and both are worth knowing before the switch. The first push was rejected before any job started, because the workflow used the `runner` context where job-level `env` is evaluated; `actionlint` reports it. The second failed in the engine tests: **INLA's posterior sampler stops without the `sn` package**, which INLA lists only as a suggestion. A machine that has `sn` for other reasons hides this. `fit_model_v2_inla()` now checks for INLA and `sn` together and names whichever is missing.

### Replay of 2026 dates {#sec-replay}

If football had been fitted by INLA on a given day in 2026, what would have been published, and how does it differ from what was?

**How.** For each date, `research/football-v2/run_replay.R` copies the football facts, the earlier stored fits and the publisher's accumulators into an isolated tree and puts that copy back as it was when production fitted (below). It then sets `engine: inla` on the league in memory and calls `fit_league()`: the production function, taking its INLA branch, with full integration and 4,000 draws as a production fit would use. Production's `extract_football_iceland()` and `publish_iceland_league()` run unchanged. Nothing under `data/` is written, and the script checks `git status` before and after to prove it.

**The store as it was.** The daily fit runs before that day's evening matches, which are ingested later and dated on the fit day. On today's store a replay would train on them and forecast nothing for them. Production records how many matches each fit saw, so the replay compares that count with the store and, where they differ by exactly the fit day's matches, moves those matches from the results back to the schedule in its copy. Each INLA fit is then checked to have trained on the same number of matches as production's fit did (@tbl-replay-cells).

**Which dates.** Production's retention keeps few stored fits. For 2026 they are the pre-season baseline fit of each sex and the last weeks of October, so those are the dates. Two more October dates (12 October for men, 4 October for women) could not be used: fixtures were rescheduled after those fits, and the publisher refuses to republish a stored fit that no longer matches the schedule. That refusal is production's own guard, working as intended.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-replay-cells
#| tbl-cap: "The replayed dates. Pre-season fits forecast the whole season (a 200-day horizon), October fits the next 14 days, as production's did. 'Returned to the schedule' are matches played on the fit day after production's fit ran. Production recorded no match count for the backfilled pre-season fits. 'Schema-valid' counts the published files that have a schema; one file per cell (the cup bracket) has none. Run times are not shown: these replays were run again after the review, on a machine shared with other work."
rc <- rp$cells
if (!is.null(rc)) {
  tab(data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[rc$sex], `As of` = rc$as_of,
    `Forecast horizon, days` = rc$horizon_days,
    `Matches the INLA fit saw` = format(rc$n_obs, big.mark = ","),
    `Production's fit saw` = ifelse(is.na(rc$production_n_obs), "not recorded", format(rc$production_n_obs, big.mark = ",")),
    `Returned to the schedule` = rc$returned_to_schedule,
    `JSON files` = rc$json_inla,
    `Schema-valid` = paste0(rc$schema_passed_inla, " of ", rc$schema_passed_inla + rc$schema_failed_inla),
    `Values compared` = format(rc$values_compared, big.mark = ","),
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

**Two comparisons, so that a difference can be given a cause.**

1. What production published that day, taken from git history, against production's own stored fit put through today's publish code. If those agree, the replay machinery is faithful, and whatever differs in the second comparison comes from the fit.
2. That baseline against the INLA replay.

#### Comparison 1: the baseline reproduces what production published

```{r}
#| label: replay-layer1
l1 <- rp$layer1_classes
l1n <- function(k) format(sum(l1$differing[l1$cause == k]), big.mark = ",")
l1_dates <- unique(rp$layer1[c("sex", "as_of")])
l1_values <- format(sum(rp$layer1_files[, "values"]), big.mark = ",")
```

For the `r nrow(l1_dates)` October dates there is a publish commit from that day. Over `r l1_values` compared values, the republished stored fit matches what production published in every number a model produces: the match forecasts, the final-position and points distributions, the team strengths, the home advantage, the cup bracket, and the league tables with their expected goals and points. `r if (!any(l1$cause == "UNEXPLAINED")) "Only two kinds of value differ, and neither depends on the fit:" else "**Unexplained differences remain; see the summary output.**"`

- **The run timestamp** (`generated_at`): `r l1n("Run timestamp")` values.
- **Rows for earlier rounds in two history files** (`final_positions_history.json`, `standings_history.json`): `r l1n("Accumulated history: earlier rounds' rows")` values. Production's publisher accumulates these files in place, round after round. A replay into an empty tree writes only the current round's rows, and those are identical.

Getting to an exact match took two corrections, and each is a fact about the pipeline worth keeping. First, the league table's expected goals and points are summed over the rounds for which a fit from before the round can still be found, and the publisher looks for that fit in two stores, the extracts and the older archive. A replay that copied only the extracts produced different sums. Second, the evening matches of the fit day, described above: on two of the four dates the published league table was one to three matches behind today's store. With the archive copied and those matches returned to the schedule, the baseline matches what was published to the last digit.

The two pre-season dates have no publish commit to compare with: those fits were backfilled, not published that day. For them the baseline is the stored fit alone.

#### Comparison 2: what the model changes

```{r}
#| label: tbl-replay-classes
#| tbl-cap: "Every value that differs between the baseline (production's stored fit) and the INLA replay, by cause, summed over the replayed dates. 'In one tree only' are entries of a distribution that one model gave no simulated draw (such an entry is left out of the file) and, in the last row, everything the pre-season baseline does not contain."
l2 <- rp$layer2_classes
why <- c(
  `Run timestamp` = "When the files were written.",
  `Team strengths` = "A different model estimates the teams. v2.0 gives each team one strength walk and a fixed style; production gives it separate attack and defence walks with its own volatility. Every published strength is a continuous estimate, so every one moves.",
  `Home advantage` = "The intended change: the home advantage is pooled and no longer forced to be positive, which removes the inflation, and its attack and defence parts are an even split by convention.",
  `Match forecasts` = "Outcome probabilities, expected goals and goal-difference distributions of the next fixtures, from the new model's rates.",
  `Season and cup simulation` = "Final-position and points distributions, simulated from the new model's strengths by production's simulator.",
  `Season simulation before the season: model and simulator` = "Pre-season dates only. The stored pre-season fits were simulated in April, before the split-season simulator existed, so their tables differ from the replay's by more than the model (below).",
  `Not in the stored baseline` = "Pre-season dates only. The stored pre-season fits were written by an earlier version of the extract and cover the top two divisions. The baseline publishes the other divisions and the cup empty, so the replay's values there have nothing to be compared with (below)."
)
if (!is.null(l2)) {
  o <- match(names(why), l2$cause)
  o <- o[!is.na(o)]
  knitr::kable(data.frame(
    Cause = l2$cause[o], `Values that differ` = format(l2$differing[o], big.mark = ","),
    `In one tree only` = format(l2$only_a[o] + l2$only_b[o], big.mark = ","),
    Files = ifelse(l2$cause[o] == "Run timestamp", "every file", gsub(".json", "", l2$surfaces[o], fixed = TRUE)),
    Why = unname(why[l2$cause[o]]),
    check.names = FALSE
  ), row.names = FALSE, align = c("l", "r", "r", "l", "l"))
}
replay_unexplained <- sum(rp$layer2$cause == "UNEXPLAINED") + sum(rp$layer1$cause == "UNEXPLAINED")
```

`r if (replay_unexplained == 0) "No value is left over. The summary script assigns every differing field to one of these causes and stops with an error if any is unassigned." else paste0("**", replay_unexplained, " fields are unassigned.**")` The timestamp row lists every file because each carries one; the model-driven rows are confined to the files named. What does *not* differ is as informative. On the October dates the league tables, including their expected goals and points, the file metadata and the number of draws are identical in the two trees, and the same files exist in both. The pre-season dates are the exception and have their own section below.

How large the model-driven differences are:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-replay-size
#| tbl-cap: "Size of the differences between production's stored fit and the INLA replay of v2.0. Outcome probabilities are home win, draw and away win of each upcoming fixture; final-position probabilities are those that changed at all (late in the season most places are already decided). On the pre-season dates the last four columns also contain the change of simulator described below, and cover the top two divisions only."
if (!is.null(rc)) {
  dash <- function(x, d = 3) ifelse(is.na(x), "–", num(x, d))
  tab(data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[rc$sex], `As of` = rc$as_of,
    Fixtures = round(rc$n_fixtures),
    `Outcome probability: mean abs.` = dash(rc$forecast_mean_abs), `largest` = dash(rc$forecast_max_abs),
    `Expected goals: mean abs.` = dash(rc$goals_mean_abs, 2),
    `Final-position probability: mean abs.` = dash(rc$place_mean_abs), `largest ` = dash(rc$place_max_abs),
    `Expected points: mean abs.` = dash(rc$points_mean_abs, 2), `largest  ` = dash(rc$points_max_abs, 2),
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-replay-ha
#| tbl-cap: "Published home advantage, averaged over teams, and its spread between teams: production's stored fit and the INLA replay. The published number is a goal ratio (1 means no home advantage)."
hd <- rp$home_advantage
if (!is.null(hd)) {
  hd <- hd[order(hd$sex, hd$as_of, match(hd$component, c("total", "offence", "defence"))), ]
  tab(data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[hd$sex], `As of` = hd$as_of,
    Component = c(total = "Total", offence = "Attack", defence = "Defence")[hd$component],
    `Production: mean` = num(hd$mean_stored, 3), `sd between teams` = num(hd$sd_stored, 3),
    `v2.0: mean` = num(hd$mean_inla, 3), `sd between teams ` = num(hd$sd_inla, 3),
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
st <- rp$strengths
st_cor <- function(component) {
  r <- st$correlation[st$component == component & st$location == "avg"]
  paste(num(min(r), 3), "to", num(max(r), 3))
}
```

Reading these:

- **Teams are ranked almost identically.** Across the replayed dates the correlation between production's and v2.0's published total strength is `r st_cor("total")`; for attack alone it is `r st_cor("offence")` and for defence `r st_cor("defence")`. The total agrees more closely than its parts, which is what a fixed style in place of two free walks should produce.
- **Home advantage falls and flattens** (@tbl-replay-ha). Production publishes a larger home advantage that varies a good deal between teams; v2.0 publishes a smaller one that is nearly the same for every team, with equal attack and defence parts. This is the inflation of @sec-ha being removed, and it is the largest visible change on the site.
- **Forecasts move by two to five points of probability on average** (@tbl-replay-size), and by as much as `r num(max(rc$forecast_max_abs, na.rm = TRUE), 2)` for one fixture. The largest moves are before the season and all go the same way, toward less extreme probabilities for last season's strongest sides: the women's 2025 champions go from 0.74 to 0.53 to win away to a side that finished mid-table, and from 0.96 to 0.83 at home to one from the lower half. That is reversion at the season break doing what it was put in to do. It is the model change, not the engine: with one model in both engines the difference was 0.002 to 0.003 (@sec-accept). The walk-forward is the evidence that the move is an improvement, and it found the gain largest in the first five rounds (@sec-model).

#### The two pre-season dates

The pre-season comparison needs more care, because its baseline is older in two ways.

```{r}
#| label: replay-preseason
pp <- rp$preseason_points
absent <- rp$absent_divisions[lengths(rp$absent_divisions) > 0]
pp_div <- if (!is.null(pp)) do.call(rbind, lapply(split(pp, list(pp$sex, pp$division), drop = TRUE), function(g) {
  per_match <- sum(g$points) / (sum(g$played) / 2)
  data.frame(
    sex = g$sex[1], division = g$division[1], teams = nrow(g), played = sum(g$played) / 2,
    implied_stored = sum(g$mean_points_stored) / per_match, implied_inla = sum(g$mean_points_inla) / per_match,
    mae_stored = mean(abs(g$mean_points_stored - g$points)), mae_inla = mean(abs(g$mean_points_inla - g$points)),
    rank_stored = stats::cor(g$mean_points_stored, g$points, method = "spearman"),
    rank_inla = stats::cor(g$mean_points_inla, g$points, method = "spearman"),
    cover_stored = mean(g$points >= g$lower_80_stored & g$points <= g$upper_80_stored),
    cover_inla = mean(g$points >= g$lower_80_inla & g$points <= g$upper_80_inla)
  )
}))
pd <- function(sex, division, column, d = 0) num(pp_div[[column]][pp_div$sex == sex & pp_div$division == division], d)
second <- pp[pp$division == "Second division", ]
second_diff <- abs(second$mean_points_inla - second$points) - abs(second$mean_points_stored - second$points)
```

- **It is partial.** The stored pre-season fits were written by an earlier version of the extract: six files where today's writes eleven, covering the top two divisions. Put through today's publish code, the baseline comes out empty for `r length(absent[[grep("^male", names(absent))[1]]])` division folders for men and `r length(absent[[grep("^female", names(absent))[1]]])` for women (the lower divisions and the cup), and those empty files fail schema validation on their own, for having no draws. The replay publishes every division and passes. Everything the replay has there, and the cup bracket file the baseline does not write at all, is the last row of @tbl-replay-classes: nothing to compare with, so nothing concluded.
- **Its season simulation is April's.** The split-season simulator arrived in July 2026. Before it, the top division was projected over the regular season alone. The arithmetic shows it: in the men's top division production's expected points add up to what `r pd("male", "Top division", "implied_stored")` matches yield, the replay's to `r pd("male", "Top division", "implied_inla")`, and `r pd("male", "Top division", "played")` were played; for women `r pd("female", "Top division", "implied_stored")`, `r pd("female", "Top division", "implied_inla")` and `r pd("female", "Top division", "played")`. In the second divisions, which do not split, both agree with the number played. So in the top division the pre-season difference in expected points (@tbl-replay-size) is mostly a change of simulator, and cannot be put down to the model.

- **In v2.0 the season simulation now starts after the break.** Since the review (finding 3 in @sec-review) the simulators are handed each team's strength at its first match of the new season: pulled toward the division mean and uncertain by the size of a winter's change, where production's projection starts from where last season ended. The largest single difference in a final-position probability on these dates is `r num(max(rc$place_max_abs[grepl("-04-", rc$as_of)]), 2)` (it was 0.18 before the fix): the title probability of last season's women's champions, 0.80 in production's pre-season projection and 0.38 in v2.0's. They went on to win the title. One outcome settles nothing either way, but it shows how much less certain v2.0 is about a season before it starts.

What compares cleanly on those dates is what the simulator does not touch: the forecasts of the opening fixtures, the strengths and the home advantage, all in the tables above.

**Which pre-season projection was closer to how the season ended?** The 2026 season is over, so both can be scored against the final table (@tbl-replay-preseason).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-replay-preseason
#| tbl-cap: "Pre-season expected points against the final 2026 table, by division: production's stored fit and the INLA replay of v2.0. Mean absolute error is in points and is comparable only in the second divisions, where both trees project the same matches; rank correlation and coverage of the 80 % interval are shown for all."
if (!is.null(pp_div)) {
  o <- order(pp_div$sex != "male", pp_div$division != "Top division")
  d <- pp_div[o, ]
  top <- d$division == "Top division"
  tab(data.frame(
    ` ` = sex_label[d$sex], Division = d$division, Teams = d$teams,
    `Mean abs. error: production` = ifelse(top, "not comparable", num(d$mae_stored, 1)),
    `v2.0` = ifelse(top, "not comparable", num(d$mae_inla, 1)),
    `Rank correlation: production` = num(d$rank_stored, 2), `v2.0 ` = num(d$rank_inla, 2),
    `80 % interval covers: production` = ifelse(top, "not comparable", paste0(round(100 * d$cover_stored), " %")),
    `v2.0  ` = paste0(round(100 * d$cover_inla), " %"),
    check.names = FALSE
  ))
}
```

Over the `r nrow(second)` teams of the two second divisions, v2.0's absolute error differs from production's by `r sgn(mean(second_diff), 2)` points (standard error `r num(stats::sd(second_diff) / sqrt(nrow(second)), 2)`; negative would favour v2.0): closer for men, further for women, and no detectable difference overall. The rank correlations also go one way for men and the other for women. One season and a few dozen teams cannot tell the two season-long projections apart. The evidence for v2.0 remains the walk-forward, which scores forecasts a week ahead, not a season ahead; a season-long comparison of the two models has not been made and would need production's model run through today's simulator.

#### What the replay establishes

The replay finds what the change of model should produce and nothing else. On every date the replay's published files pass their schemas and no field changes type. On the October dates the same files are written, and the numbers that do not depend on the fit did not move at all. On the pre-season dates the comparison is limited by an older baseline, and where it is limited this section says so.

### A reference test that needs no Stan run {#sec-reftest}

Decision 5 asks for two checks on the approximation once Stan no longer fits football every day. The weekly reference fit watches the live data. This is the other one: a test in CI that compares INLA with NUTS without running Stan. It is designed here and not yet built; it belongs with the switch, when INLA is installed where the tests run.

**What is stored.** One small file under `tests/testthat/fixtures/`, written once on a machine that has CmdStan, by a script kept next to the reference program:

- a frozen training set: the matches of one cell up to a fixed cutoff (date, teams, scores, season, division) and the fixtures after it. The women's cell to 31 July 2026 is `r format(val$dims$N[val$dims$sex == "female"], big.mark = ",")` matches and fits with INLA in seconds;
- the v2.0 options and prior values the reference was fitted with;
- what NUTS found on that training set: the hyperparameter means and quantiles, each team's state mean and sd in the last week, the league home advantage, and the outcome probabilities and expected goals of every fixture;
- how it was made: the Stan program's hash, CmdStan version, seed, number of draws, largest $\hat{R}$ and number of divergences.

**What the test does.** It rebuilds the specification from the stored training set, never from the live store, so the reference cannot go stale as matches accumulate. It fits with INLA under full integration, with a fixed seed and one thread, and compares:

| Quantity | Passes when | Seen in this report |
|---|---|---|
| Match probabilities, mean absolute difference | below 0.005 | 0.002 to 0.003 |
| Match probabilities, largest difference | below 0.025 | 0.012 to 0.014 |
| Entry-level and innovation sds | within 10 % | within 6 % |
| Near-zero sds (team home-advantage deviations) | within a factor 1.5 | 5 % to 31 % high |
| State means, mean difference in posterior sds | below 0.15 | about 0.06 |

The limits sit at about twice what was observed, so the test catches a break and not noise. They are thresholds and not snapshots because R-INLA reruns are not bit-identical.

**What it catches.** A new INLA version that changes the approximation; a change to the specification builder that silently changes the model (a prior, a structure matrix, the constraint); an adapter that maps a quantity to the wrong name, if the comparison is made on adapted quantities. The Stan program and the INLA specification are two independent implementations of one model, so their agreement is a check on both.

**What it cannot catch.** The approximation getting worse on data it has not seen, which is what the weekly reference fit and its 0.01 health warning are for; and anything wrong with the model itself, which both engines would reproduce faithfully.

**Keeping it honest.** The test first compares the stored options and priors with `football_v2_options()` and `fv2_priors()`. If the specification has changed on purpose and the reference has not been regenerated, it fails with "stale reference" and does not go on to compare numbers that no longer belong together.

### Shadow period

The football season ended on 24 October 2026; the next competitive matches are the cup's early rounds in March 2027. There is no live football to shadow until then, which shapes the plan.

| Step | When | What | Exit condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | done | Retrospective shadow: the walk-forward in this report | – |
| 1 | done, 16 November 2026 | The engine is in `R/` behind `engine: stan` (no behaviour change). A workflow for this branch only installs INLA, fits both football cells and uploads the output as an artifact. Nothing is published. | Met: INLA installs and fits on a GitHub runner, and the engine tests pass there (@sec-runner) |
| 2 | done, 16 November 2026 | Replay: for a set of 2026 dates, `fit_league()` with the INLA engine, then production's extract and publish, into an isolated tree, compared with what production published. | Met: schema validation passes and every difference is in a named class (@sec-replay) |
| 3 | from the first 2027 fixtures | Both engines fit daily. One is published, the other archived per match (this is also the immutable forecast archive the roadmap asks for). | See below |
| 4 | after cutover | Weekly reference check: the Stan program fits the same specification and its match probabilities are compared with INLA's. | Mean absolute difference below 0.01; a breach raises a health warning |

For step 3 there were two defensible orders. The owner chose the second:

- **Stan published, INLA in shadow** until a gate is met: at least 150 matches, INLA's 1X2 log loss no worse than production's by more than one standard error, schema validation green on every day, no gate failure.
- **INLA published from the first 2027 fixture, Stan in shadow** for six weeks. The evidence for the new specification is already 4,511 held-out matches, more than a spring of live shadowing would add; the pre-season baseline would come from the model that runs the season; and the off-season is when a mistake costs least.

Rollback in either case is one line (`engine: stan`): the Stan program, its gate and the layers downstream are untouched by the cutover.


## Limits {#sec-limits}

- **Five seasons, five breaks.** The results store starts in 2021. The 2022 forecasts rest on one earlier season, and everything this report says about the season break (its variance, reversion) rests on five transitions.
- **Outside benchmarks exist for 2026 only.** `r wf$priced$n[wf$priced$variant == wf$ref & wf$priced$group == "all" & wf$priced$against == "line"]` priced matches and `r wf$rounds$n[wf$rounds$variant == wf$ref & wf$rounds$group == "all"]` pre-round forecasts. Those samples resolve differences of about 0.01 in log loss, which is the size of the differences observed. Production's 2026 forecasts also include 21 May to 16 September, when a configuration bug had it training on unfiltered data.
- **Three validation cutoffs.** INLA was checked against NUTS at 31 July 2026, with five and a half seasons of data. Two early-season cutoffs were added for the hard regimes (@sec-accept); every other cutoff of the walk-forward was fitted by INLA alone.
- **Empirical Bayes in the walk-forward.** The walk-forward fixes hyperparameters at their mode and re-estimates them every fourth week. At the validation cutoff, empirical Bayes and full integration gave the same predictions to within Monte Carlo error. `r if (!is.null(res$hyper_check)) paste0("Re-estimating every week instead, on the women's 2026 season (", res$hyper_check$n, " matches), moved match probabilities by ", num(res$hyper_check$mean_abs_dp, 4), " on average, the 1X2 score by ", sgn(res$hyper_check$d_1x2), " (se ", num(res$hyper_check$se_1x2, 4), ") and the scoreline score by ", sgn(res$hyper_check$d_scoreline), " (se ", num(res$hyper_check$se_scoreline, 4), "). Production would re-estimate at every fit, so if anything the walk-forward understates the model.") else "The four-weekly cadence itself was not compared with weekly re-estimation."`
- **The reversion coefficient is fixed in INLA.** It sits inside the precision matrix, where INLA cannot estimate it without a custom latent model. The value used was chosen before looking at the data, from published between-season memory of 0.74 to 0.80.
- **Timings.** Four model-fitting sessions shared this machine all evening, so sampler effort is reported as leapfrog steps and divergences, which do not depend on load. The run times in @tbl-timing were taken last, with no other model fit running, but with macOS background sync still using about 2.5 cores; an earlier run under heavier load gave 7 and 14 seconds for INLA where this one gave 6 and 11. The re-runs after the review (@sec-rerun) shared the machine with other work, so no run time from them is reported.
- **INLA on a GitHub runner is tested for one version on one image.** INLA 25.06.07 on `ubuntu-latest` with R 4.5.3 (@sec-runner). A newer INLA, or a new runner image, is a new test.
- **The replay covers the ends of the season, not the middle.** Production's retention keeps few stored fits: for 2026 they are the pre-season baseline and the last weeks of October. Two more October dates could not be used because fixtures were rescheduled after those fits and the publisher refuses, correctly, to republish a stored fit that no longer matches the schedule. No mid-season date was replayed. The two pre-season baselines come from an earlier version of the extract, cover the top two divisions and predate the split-season simulator, so on those dates the season-long projections of the two models cannot be compared like for like; that comparison needs production's model run through today's simulator, which means a Stan fit that was not made.
- **Fixtures with a new team are skipped**, as in production: a team with no match in the training set gets no forecast. In the men's data that is the fourth division.
- **Not run.** A style term that walks instead of the fixed one; division offsets combined with the promotion shock on the recommended model (the only combined run was the void one); offsets and league walks together; reversion values other than 0.7 and 0.8 on the walk-forward; the walk-forward under full integration (it used empirical Bayes throughout); a second cutoff with one season of history.
- **Structural choices at this sample size, and one unreconciled comparison.** Where two structures could not be separated on Icelandic data, the report says so. A test bed of eight large European leagues finds a much smaller gain from strength plus style than this report does. @sec-tests shows the two agree where they are comparable and lists what would settle the rest; that test has not been run. The European figures are research-only and stay in `/Users/brynjolfurjonsson/.claude-reviews/sports-pan-european/structural-tests.md`.
- **Part of the selection ladder predates two of the review's fixes.** The recommended model, the reference and the two models that bracket the reversion were run again on the fixed code (@sec-rerun). The other `r length(stale)` reversion models of the ladder were not, and neither was the split of the strength-and-style gain by season and competition: those comparisons are between runs from before the fix. On the models that were re-run the fix moved no paired comparison by more than `r num(max(abs(hl$new - hl$old)[1:6]), 4)`.
- **v2.0 was chosen on the matches it was scored on.** Hence the re-examination on 2027 matches due 15 July 2027 (@sec-model).
